title: Segment Anything Pancreas: A Unified MRI Segmentation Model for Pancreatic Cancer Radiotherapy
abstract: Background: Limited tumor annotations and incomplete labels across MRI datasets hinder unified segmentation of pancreatic tumors and organs at risk (OARs) for MRI-guided radiotherapy. Purpose: We propose Pancreas-MedNeXt, a unified model that segments the whole pancreas, its subregions, tumors, and surrounding OARs from one MRI volume. Methods: The model uses a shared MedNeXt encoder-decoder with supervised whole-pancreas and subregion pretraining, followed by multitask fine-tuning. Three output heads predict the pancreatic subregions, tumor, and OARs (stomach, duodenum, kidneys). An annotation-aware loss allows training on partially labeled data without treating unannotated structures as background. Pancreas and tumor were evaluated by three-fold cross-validation on 142 PANTHER patients (92 diagnostic, 50 MR-Linac), subregions and OARs on Cyst-X and AMOS test sets, and pancreas and OARs on 33 external T1-weighted TotalSegmentator scans. Comparisons with nnU-Net, MedNeXt, VISTA3D, and Swin UNETR used the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with paired bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: Pancreas-MedNeXt achieved the highest mean pancreas and tumor DSC on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI. Tumor DSC was 58.41% and 42.55%, exceeding task-specific MedNeXt by 4.94 (95% CI: 0.28-9.45) and 5.89 (95% CI: 2.37-9.72) percentage points, respectively. Whole-pancreas DSC was 85.73% and 70.66%. Pretraining improved head, body, and tail DSC by 2.01, 3.00, and 3.78 percentage points over training from scratch. It also achieved the highest DSC for the pancreas, duodenum, and right kidney on AMOS, and for all five organs on external MRI, exceeding the next-best method by 4.92-8.85 percentage points.Conclusion: A single Pancreas-MedNeXt model segments tumors, pancreatic subregions, and OARs on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI, which could streamline contouring for pancreatic cancer radiotherapy.

title: A General-Purpose Adaptable Foundation Model for Total-Body PET Kinetic Modelling
abstract: Voxel-level kinetic modeling in total-body dynamic positron emission tomography (TB-PET) enables precise physiological quantification but complicates parameter uncertainty estimation. While generative consistency models (CMs) can rapidly estimate Bayesian posterior distributions, they are constrained by type of tracers, kinetic models, and protocols. Training them from scratch whenever a new tracer, model or protocol is used can be computationally intensive. To address this, we introduce LoRACM, a parameter-efficient framework utilizing low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to transfer a pretrained foundation CM to novel TB-PET scenarios. We evaluated three adaptation scenarios using simulated and human data: scanner and protocol transfer for FDG two-tissue compartment modeling; FP-CIT simplified reference tissue modeling; and high-temporal-resolution FDG blood flow imaging via the adiabatic approximation to tissue homogeneity model. Each adaptation was trained in less than 3 hours on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU using 50,000 simulated pairs. In simulations, LoRACM showed strong agreement with results from Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, which we use as reference posterior distributions), yielding median Kullback-Leibler divergences of 0.05-0.11 and median absolute percentage errors below 1.2% for each kinetic parameter of interest. In human data, LoRACM generated total-body K_i maps comparable to the ones made by non-negative nonlinear least squares (NNLS) fitting and a consistency model trained from scratch. Striatal dopamine binding potential estimates predicted by LoRACM correlated with NNLS estimates (r = 0.968-0.988). LoRACM produced total-body blood flow imaging with FDG matching the one made by NNLS. These underscore the potential of adapting a pretrained CM with LoRA for fast and reliable posterior parameter inference for kinetic models across distinct TB-PET applications.

title: MATS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Controllable and Reflective Tumor Synthesis
abstract: Synthesizing realistic tumors on medical images helps address data scarcity for clinical AI. Existing diffusion-based methods, however, lack fine-grained attribute-level controllability, closed-loop quality verification, and awareness of which morphological patterns are underrepresented in the target distribution. We present MATS, a multi-agent framework for text-controllable, cross-organ tumor synthesis. Given a target disease, MATS first profiles its morphological distribution over a fine-grained attribute space covering tumor geometry and appearance, and constructs a generation plan that amplifies underrepresented subtypes while keeping common ones dominant. It then localizes the target organ, proposes anatomically valid placement, and executes two-stage diffusion to produce the tumor mask and render texture, each conditioned on the corresponding attributes. A closed-loop reflective mechanism verifies attribute alignment at three checkpoints throughout synthesis and provides targeted feedback to guide re-generation when misalignment is detected. Trained exclusively on a single-source pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor dataset, MATS consistently improves downstream segmentation both in-domain and across LiTS, KiTS, and MSD-Pancreas benchmarks, whereas most prior generative augmentation methods fall below real-only training.

title: Bayesian PET Reconstruction with Learned Flow Matching Priors via Langevin Sampling
abstract: Image reconstruction for positron emission tomography (PET) is a challenging inverse problem due to its inherent ill-posedness and Poisson counting noise, particularly in low-dose acquisitions. In this work, we introduce a novel Bayesian PET reconstruction framework that leverages a flow-matching generative prior learned from high-quality PET images. By incorporating this prior, we formulate PET reconstruction as a Bayesian inference problem and solve it via latent-space posterior sampling using the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. We evaluate the proposed method through numerical experiments and benchmark it against classical reconstruction methods and state-of-the-art deep learning-based baselines. The proposed method achieves improved reconstruction performance while enabling posterior uncertainty quantification.
venue: 2026 IEEE Image, Video, and Multidimensional Signal Processing Workshop (IVMSP)

title: Task-Performance Routing for Multi-Teacher Distillation in CT Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Pre-trained models offer complementary strengths in CT organ segmentation, but their relative accuracy varies across organs and spatial regions. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation can combine these strengths in a single student, yet global or instance-level teacher weights overlook variation within a 3D volume. We propose Task-Performance Routing (TPR), which uses region-wise segmentation errors to determine teacher weights during training without learned routing parameters. In hard regions, TPR favors teachers with lower prediction errors; in easy regions, it uses uniform weights to combine their knowledge. A hierarchical spatial partition provides fine-grained routing in shallow encoder stages and coarse-grained routing in deep stages. Experiments on BTCV, MSD-Liver, and MSD-Pancreas with two teacher pairs and two backbone architectures show higher Dice scores than the individual teachers, adaptive ensembles, and evaluated multi-teacher distillation baselines. On MSD-Pancreas, TPR achieves Dice scores of 65.40% with SwinUNETR and 68.25% with U-Net, compared with 64.38% and 67.45% for the corresponding adaptive ensembles. Inference uses the student alone, with no routing or teacher overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/EdvinCecilia/TPR_MultiTeacher.

title: VariaFlow: Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
abstract: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection no longer fails at reconstruction. Generative models produce high-quality pseudo-healthy reconstructions, and the remaining difficulty is the step of scoring residuals. The residual between a scan and its reconstruction has two indistinguishable sources, genuine pathology and the anatomical variation that separates one healthy brain from another. Scoring against a single reconstruction treats both as anomalous, inflating false positives where healthy anatomy varies most while small or subtle lesions are lost in the surrounding reconstruction error. We identify the missing quantity as the predictive variance, how much a healthy reconstruction can vary at each location. We introduce VariaFlow, which estimates this variance from an ensemble of mask-guided restorations under an unconditional flow matching prior, each started from a different noise initialization, and which normalizes the residual by the resulting standard deviation. Few-step flow matching keeps the ensemble computationally affordable, and restoring at two spatial scales captures lesions of different size. Across three brain MRI datasets spanning stroke and tumor, VariaFlow is trained once on healthy anatomy and generalizes across all three, attaining the highest AUROC (0.94, 0.80, 0.78) on each and the highest AUPRC on both cross-domain datasets, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37% and 50%. Under domain shift, the same baseline drops by up to 52% in AUPRC, whereas VariaFlow stays more stable and achieves the best small-lesion Dice on all three datasets.

title: Roadmap: Image reconstruction in emission tomography for the era of fast Monte Carlo simulation
abstract: Quantitative image reconstruction in positron emission tomography and single photon emission computed tomography depends on how accurately the forward model describes photon emission, transport and detection. Monte Carlo simulation is the most complete model available, yet it is mostly used as an offline reference rather than inside the reconstruction. This roadmap asks what it would take to change that. The main obstacle is not only simulation time. Iterative reconstruction requires the expectation of the measured data and the gradient of the data fidelity, whereas Monte Carlo simulation produces noisy realisations of a complete acquisition. GPU implementations, variance reduction and learned surrogate models have made simulations much faster. At the same time, modern scanners acquire ever larger data sets with larger system models, and further gains in quantitative accuracy require more detailed physics. We discuss how fast Monte Carlo simulation can improve the modelling of the system response, scatter, positron range and the joint estimation of activity and attenuation, how noisy simulations can enter reconstruction algorithms, and which computing hardware makes this feasible. Monte Carlo simulation is most valuable where analytic models fail, and most practical solutions will combine both. The most immediate benefit of fast simulators is the validation and calibration of faster analytic models, together with more accurate, absolutely quantitative scatter estimates. Key open problems are the use of noisy simulations as expectations, in particular for sparse data, the computation of gradients and adjoints, the allocation of a limited simulation budget, and the use of scattered events as a source of information rather than a nuisance. Faster simulators are necessary but not sufficient, and progress requires simulators and reconstruction methods to be developed together.

title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules
abstract: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.

title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

title: Measuring What Matters: A Causal Reliance Score for Histopathology Image Segmentation
abstract: Reliable histopathology segmentation requires models that rely on pathology-relevant structures rather than spurious background correlations. In this work, we argue that improving architectures alone is insufficient if models continue to rely on spurious correlations rather than pathology-relevant features. We introduce a causality-inspired evaluation framework based on controlled interventions that explicitly probes model sensitivity to foreground tissue structure and background/domain variation. Building on this, we propose the Causal Reliance Score (CRS), a metric that quantifies the relative sensitivity of model predictions to foreground perturbation versus background/domain variation under controlled interventions. To support this analysis, we design augmentation strategies that act as implicit counterfactual interventions during training, encouraging invariance to nuisance factors while preserving morphology. We demonstrate how these interventions reveal behavioural differences between models that are not captured by standard metrics such as Dice or IoU. While we instantiate our framework using a self-supervised transformer (CAUSE-ViT), the primary contribution of this work is not a new architecture, but a principled intervention-based methodology and evaluation metric for auditing model behaviour in medical image segmentation. Our results suggest that evaluating model behaviour through counterfactual interventions is essential for developing reliable and clinically robust medical image segmentation systems.

title: Quantitative Ultrasound Characterizes Perfusion Trajectories in Healthy and Inflamed Gingival Wound Healing
abstract: Rationale and Objectives: Visual examination of extraction-site healing provides limited insight into underlying vascular recovery. We developed a quantitative ultrasound framework to assess gingival perfusion and persistent inflammation. Materials and Methods: Patients (n = 51) undergoing extraction and socket preservation were imaged longitudinally using color-flow ultrasound and laser speckle contrast analysis (LASCA) from 2 weeks to 3 months after extraction. Pre-scan-converted Total Recall Imaging (TRI) data with phase information were processed using scan conversion, bilateral filtering, and power estimation to derive velocity-weighted color pixel density (CPDvel). Gingival regions of interest were automatically segmented using deep learning and assessed with Dice and Bland-Altman analyses. CPDvel was compared between healthy and inflamed visits in early (<35 days) and recovery (>35 days) periods and with LASCA. Results: Segmentation achieved a mean Dice score of 0.98 and median of 0.99 (IQR, 0.98-0.99), with minimal area bias (-0.005%; 95% limits of agreement, -1.68% to 1.67%). Median CPDvel decreased by 81% between early and recovery periods in healthy visits (p = 0.01), compared with a nonsignificant 26% reduction in inflamed visits (p = 0.31). During recovery, CPDvel was higher in inflamed than healthy visits (0.12 vs 0.03 cm/s; p = 0.04). LASCA showed smaller reductions (13% and 9%, respectively). CPDvel was positively correlated with LASCA in healthy (one-sided p = 0.03) and inflamed visits (one-sided p = 0.13). Conclusions: TRI-based quantitative ultrasound enabled automated perfusion assessment with reduced dependence on scanner display settings. Distinct perfusion patterns and more pronounced temporal changes than LASCA support its potential for noninvasive monitoring of oral wound healing and persistent inflammation.

title: Think Before You Locate: Clinical Chain-of-Though Supervision for Sequential Medical Image Grounding
abstract: Clinicians rarely localize a finding from one image alone. They compare current and prior scans, follow structures across slices, and match regions across views or modalities. Yet vision-language models for sequential medical grounding usually learn only from bounding boxes. Boxes show where the target is, but they do not explain why that region in that image answers the question. We study whether explicit, image-grounded reasoning can improve localization, and which tasks benefit from it. We introduce method, whose core is MedChain, a corpus of 182,573 filtered rationales spanning eight sequential grounding tasks and ten imaging modalities. A medical VLM (FlemingVL-38B) first drafts a caption-like rationale, and a multimodal refiner (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) then re-examines the images, question and annotated box to write a box-conditioned explanation with explicit cross-image reasoning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 on these rationales with deliberative chain-of-thought supervision (dCoT-SFT). Across 4B, 9B, and 27B models, dCoT-SFT sets a new state of the art on MedSG-Bench. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5, improving over the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points. In a paired comparison using fixed 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13--4.00). The gains mainly come from change detection and object tracking, while performance drops on three appearance-matching tasks. Replacing a model's own rationale with a rationale from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points, showing that localization depends strongly on the reasoning context. Finally, adding GRPO with an IoU reward after dCoT-SFT gives only small and task-dependent gains, which we analyze through controlled multi-seed development experiments.

title: BreastXAgent: A lightweight agentic explainability framework for breast density classification
abstract: Deep learning models for breast density classification typically return only a label and confidence score. This paper presents BreastXAgent, a lightweight agentic framework that combines a pretrained classifier, Grad-CAM visual explanation, LangGraph-based routing, LLM report generation, and rule-based guardrails to produce controlled, faithful, non-diagnostic reports. On 160 mammography images, uncontrolled LLM reporting produced 75% Grad-CAM overclaims and 62.5% clinical overclaims. Strict prompting and LangGraph routing improved safety but did not eliminate violations. The full BreastXAgent achieved 100% safety pass rate, zero overclaims, and highest utility score. Results demonstrate that agentic guardrails enable safe, structured explanation generation without modifying the underlying classifier.
venue: Proc. SPIE 14346, Third International Conference on Frontiers of Applied Optics and Computer Engineering (AOCE 2026), 143460I (2026)

title: AdaptAD: Foundation Model Adaptation with Missing Modality Robustness for Alzheimer's Disease Staging Across the Disease Continuum
abstract: Staging Alzheimer's disease (AD) across its continuum, from cognitively normal (CN) through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia from a single structural MRI remains difficult because 3-D networks overfit small cohorts, and FreeSurfer morphometry is often unavailable. We present AdaptAD, which reads a registered T1-weighted scan as 16 anatomically placed 2.5-D slices through the medial temporal lobe and adapts a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), training 3.5 M of 89 M parameters. Morphometry enters as tokens when present, or as a learned [MISSING] token, and a missing-aware stacker fuses both experts. Under a pre-registered protocol, ten methods were compared for three-class CN/MCI/AD staging on identical 5-fold splits of 597 ADNI participants, 29% without FreeSurfer, with Holm-corrected paired bootstrap tests. The locked model was tested once on 993 OASIS-3 participants (988 scored by every method). On ADNI, AdaptAD achieved a three-class macro-AUC of 0.745 (95% CI 0.709 to 0.781), ranking first and significantly exceeding full fine-tuning, ShaSpec and a 3-D CNN. On OASIS-3 it reached 0.780 (0.748 to 0.814), and on the CDR-based label (0.804) it significantly outperformed every 3-D and image-tabular method. LoRA matched full fine-tuning with 25 times fewer trainable parameters, and removing morphometry changed external macro-AUC by less than 0.003. The disease score tracked MMSE and CDR-SB within diagnostic groups and stratified MCI-to-dementia progression (log-rank p < 0.001), while saliency concentrated in medial temporal and periventricular regions. A parameter-efficient 2-D foundation model can therefore stage the full AD continuum from a routine T1 scan without morphometry, offering a scalable route to memory-clinic deployment.

title: A Novel Lightweight Multi-Scale Branching Encoder for Few-Shot Image Classification
abstract: Few-Shot Learning (FSL) addresses classification scenarios in which only a small number of labeled examples are available for each class. This paper presents the Sum12 Multi-Scale branching encoder, a lightweight convolutional architecture designed to improve the embedding stage of Prototypical Networks without substantially increasing computational cost. The encoder uses seven parallel convolutional branches whose kernel-size combinations sum to 12, allowing local and broader spatial structures to be represented within a unified Multi-Scale feature space. The proposed architecture was evaluated on Omniglot, CIFAR- FS, FC100, and miniImageNet under controlled few-shot learning protocols and compared with the original Prototypical Network encoder and Inception-inspired branch variants. Additional ablation studies have investigated fusion strategies, dilated convolutions, branch compositions, and receptive field budget. Beyond few-shot learning, the encoder was also tested on the MedMNIST 2D benchmark to assess its behavior in conventional supervised medical image classification. Across these experiments, Sum12 generally improved the low-shot classification performance with respect to the basic ProtoNet encoder while preserving a compact model size. These properties suggest that the proposed encoder may be suitable for low-data visual recognition and resource-constrained intelligent imaging applications. However, complete end-to- end validation on the target embedded platform, including resolution of the observed implementation discrepancies, remains future work.

title: Predicting Cognitive Profiles from Structural MRI using Spatial Graph Representation Learning
abstract: Predicting cognitive abilities from structural neuroimaging remains challenging due to the high dimensionality and geometric complexity of brain morphology. Conventional models typically flatten regional morphometry into tabular features, failing to explicitly represent spatial relationships. We propose a Spatial-Topological Graph Neural Network (ST-GNN) to predict four distinct cognitive phenotypes across large pediatric cohorts (N = 2,378 to 2,424). By projecting regional morphometry onto a population-level standardized spatial graph, ST-GNN restricts message passing to defined neighboring regions. Evaluations demonstrate that ST-GNN effectively fuses spatial morphology with systemic covariates, outperforming linear baselines and topology-free deep models. Ablations reveal that imposing a sparse geometric topology (K-nearest neighbors) and utilizing global feature scaling - which preserves absolute morphometric scale - outperform fully connected networks and region-normalized approaches. These choices provide transferable architectural inductive biases, revealing differences between computational routing and morphometric feature attribution. Integrated Gradients analysis identified distinct morphological features consistent with neuroanatomical evidence, such as cerebellar volume for working memory and superior frontal surface area for executive function. These findings suggest standardized structural MRI provides useful information for task-specific cognitive prediction, establishing a foundation for MRI-based neurodevelopmental assessment.

title: Toward Contrast-Free Breast MRI: Improving Cancer Detection With Virtual Contrast Enhanced Imaging
abstract: Although contrast-enhanced (CE) breast MRI is an important tool for cancer detection, intravenous gadolinium administration introduces additional considerations for patients and clinical workflows. AI based virtual contrast enhanced (VCE) MRI could help identify patients for whom acquired CE imaging may be avoidable without compromising diagnostic performance. We developed a framework that combines non contrast (NC) and VCE MRI predictions for cancer detection. On the held-out test set, cancer detection using NC MRI alone achieved an AUROC of 0.865. Combining the predictions from NC and VCE MRI improved AUROC to 0.901. Building on this complementary predictive value, we evaluated patient-level routing to progressively replace acquired CE examinations with the NC plus VCE pathway, prioritizing patients with the most confident NC predictions. This simulation suggests that diagnostic performance can be largely preserved while limiting acquired CE imaging to approximately 40% of patients. Together, these findings demonstrate the complementary value of VCE MRI and suggest its potential to support selective contrast use in breast cancer screening.

title: Directional Dual-Head Supervision for Real-Time Source-Free Polyp Segmentation
abstract: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is critical for medical image segmentation as it adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing source data, thereby preserving data privacy. However, its effectiveness is often limited by confirmation bias: self-training models tend to miss small polyps, hallucinate foreground, and produce imprecise contours. We propose MedRT-SFSeg, a real-time SFDA framework built on a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture. Mask-DHF fuses precision- and recall-oriented predictions into stable pseudo-instances, while DURR uses the sign of pixel-level dual-head disagreement as a directional cue to expand or shrink masks, and additionally recovers missed instances and suppresses hallucinations. Seg-MARD further regularizes feature representations through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling. Experiments on bidirectional adaptation between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB show that MedRT-SFSeg achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice and 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, improving the non-adapted baseline by 7.7 and 9.8 Dice points while running at more than 62 FPS end-to-end. These results suggest that segmentation-aware dual-head supervision can improve pseudo-label quality without sacrificing real-time inference. Project page: https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg

title: A generative foundation model for computational brain imaging
abstract: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.

title: Evaluating SAM-based and Convolutional Architectures in Thin Retinal Vessel Segmentation: Model Capacity, Computational Cost and Foundation Pre-training
abstract: In retinal vessel segmentation, plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) are commonly expected to perform worse than convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on thin vessels, for reasons such as their coarse patch tokenization, their weak locality bias and their need for large training sets. Although this expectation is widely shared in the literature, how plain ViTs actually compare with CNNs on thin vessels has not been systematically quantified. We address this question by comparing a model with a plain ViT encoder (MedSAM), a hybrid Transformer (LiteMedSAM) and three CNNs of different sizes on three retinal datasets (DRIVE, HRF, FIVES) and, as a second-domain check, a microscopy dataset (VessMap). We measured the centerline recall and precision of thin vessels and compared the models while also considering their computational cost and how many epochs they needed to train. We found that the pre-trained MedSAM had a centerline recall of thin vessels that was not significantly different from that of the best CNN on all four datasets (-0.6 to +2.5 percentage points). A compact plain ViT obtained through architecture search but trained from scratch did not retain this performance. For pre-trained plain ViTs, our results do not support the expectation that they miss thin vessels, although similar thin-vessel performance can be obtained with much smaller models.

title: CheXPoT: Post-Hoc Visual Verification and Correction of VLM-Generated Radiology Reports
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.

title: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where each cell sits in the tissue. The inverse, what a given transcriptomic state looks like, is less explored but equally useful: it lets researchers visualize the morphological consequence of a molecular state and interpret a spatial assay's molecular calls against real tissue structure. GeneFlow, the current state of the art on the Xenium gene expression-to-image benchmark, trains a model from scratch, incurring a high cost on every new target dataset it is applied to. We instead propose GESTALT, which reformulates gene expression-to-image synthesis as predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding. A lightweight gene-token transformer predicts this embedding from multi-cell gene expression, and a frozen or LoRA-adapted diffusion decoder (PixCell) renders it as an image. Because this visual knowledge is reused rather than relearned, GESTALT trains in a fraction of the time. In both multi-cell and single-cell settings, our method outperforms the SoTA on perceptual metrics across all three Xenium datasets. Beyond improved image quality, GESTALT natively synthesizes at 1024 x 1024, and is evaluated in three generalization settings: zero-shot transfer across gene panels and datasets, held-out patients and disease states, and transfer across studies and tissue sources. Coupled with a statistical model of spatial expression, GESTALT also provides, to our knowledge, the first paired synthesis of cell-resolved transcriptomic fields and tissue images with explicit control over cell type, density, and composition. Code is available at https://github.com/trongnhandev1011/Gestalt.

title: Modeling Fat-shift for Improved Head Segmentation from MRI Scans using a Probabilistic Model
abstract: Personalized computational head models for biophysical simulations rely on accurate whole-head segmentations from T1-weighted (T1w) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. While T1w scans provide excellent contrast for intracranial anatomy, extracerebral tissues have partly almost no signal (compact bone) and also suffer from the so-called chemical shift artifact, which affects the fatty tissues in MRI and causes them to spatially shift in the frequency encoding direction of the scan. This artifact occurs primarily in two structures of the head: the spongy bone, a fatty compartment inside the compact bone, and the subcutaneous fat, located directly underneath the skin. The frequency-encoding direction is often set in the superior-inferior direction, causing the fatty tissues to shift down and, as a result, making the skull appear thinner than it actually is. Existing segmentation methods do not model this artifact, consequently leading to inaccurate labeling of the skull and scalp, which introduces a bias in biophysical simulations. The direction and magnitude of the fat-shift can be determined from the scan parameters, thus making it possible to explicitly model the shift and to recover the correct anatomy. This study introduces a probabilistic model that uses variational inference to segment head and brain structures from a T1w scan while accounting for the fat-shift artifact. The proposed Fat-shift-informed Label Optimization of the Whole head (FLOW) method reconstructs extracerebral anatomy more accurately than a fat-shift-agnostic segmentation approach while maintaining high segmentation accuracy in all other structures. FLOW-based fat-shift corrected segmentations significantly reduce bias in electric field simulations compared to a segmentation method that does not model the shift.

title: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease: The NOPARK Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Importance Nicotinamide riboside, a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide precursor, has been proposed as a potential disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson disease based on preclinical and early studies. Whether prolonged oral nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease is unknown. Objective To determine whether nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease compared with placebo. Design, setting, and participants Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial conducted at 11 centers in Norway. Eligible participants were patients aged 35 years or older with Parkinson disease diagnosed within 2 years before enrollment, Hoehn and Yahr disease stage less than 3, abnormal dopamine transporter scintigraphy findings confirming dopaminergic nigrostriatal denervation, and stable dopaminergic treatment before enrollment. Of 537 screened individuals, 410 were randomized from May 6, 2020, to June 20, 2024, and 393 were included in the primary analysis. Final follow-up was completed on June 19, 2025. Interventions Patients were randomized to receive oral nicotinamide riboside, 500 mg twice daily (n = 206), or matching placebo (n = 204) for 52 weeks. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was change from baseline to week 52 in the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale total score (MDS-UPDRS parts I-III; range, 0-236, with higher scores indicating more severe disease; clinically important differences for improvement and worsening, 6.7 and 5.2 points, respectively), analyzed using a mixed model for repeated measures. The 5 key secondary outcomes were the individual parts I, II, and III of the MDS-UPDRS; dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography brain imaging findings; and the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale score (NMSS; range, 0-360, with higher scores indicating greater nonmotor symptom burden). Results Among the 393 participants in the primary analysis, the mean age was 65.6 (SD, 9.4) years and 133 (34%) were female. At week 52, the total MDS-UPDRS score increased by 2.45 (95% CI, 0.80-4.10) points with nicotinamide riboside and decreased by 0.27 (95% CI, -1.95 to 1.40) points with placebo, yielding an adjusted mean difference of 2.72 points (95% CI, 0.47-4.98 points; P = .02), favoring placebo. Of the 5 prespecified key secondary outcomes, 4 showed no significant difference, but nonmotor symptom burden worsened more with nicotinamide riboside (NMSS score adjusted mean difference, 4.22 [95% CI, 1.07-7.37] points; P = .009). Serious adverse events occurred in 17 (8.3%) of 205 participants receiving nicotinamide riboside and 29 (14.1%) of 205 receiving placebo in the safety population. Conclusions and relevance Among patients with early Parkinson disease, nicotinamide riboside treatment for 52 weeks did not improve clinical outcomes and was associated with worse clinical outcomes than placebo. These findings do not support nicotinamide riboside as a disease-modifying treatment for Parkinson disease. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03568968.

title: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform.
abstract: Importance Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited. Objective To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries. Design, setting, and participants This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries. Main outcomes and measures The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined. Results Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians. Conclusions and relevance Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.

title: Roxadustat Treatment After PCI Among Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Importance Preclinical studies suggest that stabilization of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) may attenuate reperfusion injury. Objective To determine whether oral roxadustat, a HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, reduced infarct size when administered after reperfusion among patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Design, setting, and participants This phase 2, open-label, randomized clinical trial-Effect of Roxadustat in Acute Myocardial Infarction (ROXAMI)-enrolled adults with STEMI undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) at a single tertiary medical center between April 1, 2021, and March 31, 2024, with follow-up through 1 year. Interventions Oral roxadustat (100 mg, 3 times per week for 2 weeks), initiated within 2 hours after primary PCI, or standard care alone. Main outcomes and measures The primary end point was infarct size as a percentage of the left ventricle at 30 days measured by late gadolinium enhancement on [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Prespecified secondary end points included major adverse cardiovascular events, myocardial injury markers, echocardiographic parameters, and myocardial fibroblast activation parameters on [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET and MRI. The primary efficacy analysis for infarct size was conducted in the modified intention-to-treat population. Results Among 158 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 63.6 [11.0] years; 133 men [84.2%]; 79 randomized to each group), 148 (93.7%; 72 roxadustat and 76 control) had evaluable imaging for the primary outcome. For the primary end point, mean (SD) infarct size did not significantly differ between the roxadustat and control groups (23.3% [12.2%] vs 22.0% [12.2%]; mean difference, 1.3 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.7 to 5.3 percentage points; P = .51). Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 3 of 79 patients (3.8%) in the roxadustat group and 7 of 79 (8.9%) in the control group (hazard ratio, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.11-1.63; P = .21). In multiplicity-unadjusted secondary analyses, adjusted between-group differences at 12 months were 2.9 percentage points (95% CI, 0.4-5.3 percentage points; P = .02) for the change in left ventricular ejection fraction (mean [SD]: roxadustat, 3.4% [0.9%] vs control, 0.5% [0.9%]) and -4.5 mL/m2 (95% CI, -8.9 to -0.1 mL/m2; P = .045) for left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (mean [SD]: roxadustat, 1.2 [1.6] mL/m2 vs control, 5.7 [1.6] mL/m2). The incidence of prespecified safety end points did not differ between the roxadustat and control groups. Conclusions and relevance In this randomized clinical trial of patients with STEMI, roxadustat administration after PCI did not significantly reduce infarct size at 30 days compared with control. Secondary ventricular remodeling findings were exploratory and require confirmation. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04803864.

title: Gain-of-Function Variants in PLAAT4 and Spinal Predominant Demyelinating Leukodystrophy.
abstract: Importance Leukoencephalopathies are clinically and etiologically heterogeneous disorders, and establishing a specific diagnosis remains challenging. Patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and brain white matter hyperintensities (WMH) may be misdiagnosed as having multiple sclerosis, potentially exposing them to unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy. Objective To define the clinical, radiological, and genetic features of spinal predominant demyelinating leukodystrophy with leg spasticity (SPDMLS). Design, setting, and participants This case series involved participants from 4 tertiary referral hospitals within the China Alliance for Rare Diseases during the period July 2019 to August 2025. The study design integrated clinical evaluations and whole-exome sequencing (WES), as well as targeted plasma lipidomics correlated with SPATAX-EUROSPA disability stages. Variant pathogenicity was evaluated using an oligodendrocyte-specific knock-in mouse model. Participants were patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and central nervous system (CNS) WMH and available family members, including presymptomatic carriers. Exposures WES, genetic characterization, testing. Main outcomes and measures Identification of disease-associated gene and characterization of clinical, radiological, and genetic features of SPDMLS. Results Twenty-six individuals from 11 unrelated families were included; 4 patients underwent longitudinal follow-up for up to 5 years. Recurrent heterozygous PLAAT4 (phospholipase A and acyltransferase 4) variants (p.I14T and p.A96V) were associated with a novel autosomal dominant leukoencephalopathy, named SPDMLS. Age at onset was 11 to 51 years (median [IQR], 22 [15-29] years), with patients predominantly developing spastic paraplegia. Symbol Digit Modalities Test scores ranged from 11 to 70 in 6 available patients. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated slow progression with heterogeneous brain WMH and a stereotyped pattern of symmetric, long-segment "girdle-like" spinal cord WMH accompanied by atrophy. Somatosensory- and motor-evoked potentials indicated dysfunction of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, respectively. In presymptomatic carriers, spinal cord signal alterations preceded brain involvement. An oligodendrocyte-specific knock-in mouse model provided in vivo functional evidence supporting a role of PLAAT4 gain-of-function in driving demyelination, informing SPDMLS pathogenesis. Patient plasma lipidomics suggested accumulation of arachidonic acid-related lipids correlating with disability stage. Conclusions and relevance This study found that PLAAT4 variants delineated SPDMLS, a clinically distinct leukodystrophy that should be considered in patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and CNS WMH. Arachidonic acid-related lipids represent a candidate biomarker for disease progression.

title: Neoadjuvant Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Before Inferior Vena Cava Thrombectomy for Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Importance Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with inferior vena cava (IVC) tumor thrombus is associated with substantial perioperative risk and frequent recurrence despite nephrectomy and thrombectomy. No established neoadjuvant local therapy exists for this high-risk population. Objective To evaluate the feasibility, safety, clinical outcomes, and exploratory biomarker effects of neoadjuvant stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) targeting IVC tumor thrombus before nephrectomy and thrombectomy. Design, setting, and participants This single-center prospective phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial enrolled patients with newly diagnosed RCC and Mayo level II to IV IVC tumor thrombus eligible for neoadjuvant SABR and definitive surgery from July 2015 to January 2024. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to August 2026. Intervention Neoadjuvant SABR to the radiographically defined IVC tumor thrombus, delivered as 40 Gy in 5 fractions or 36 Gy in 3 fractions, followed by radical nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy. Main outcomes and measures The primary end point was 1-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) compared with a prespecified historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7%. Secondary outcomes included 90-day perioperative morbidity and mortality, adverse events, pulmonary embolism, overall survival, and cancer-specific survival. Exploratory analyses included Ki-67 immunohistochemistry and tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA. Results Of 23 patients who received neoadjuvant SABR, 22 completed surgery, and 21 were included in the primary RFS analysis. Of 21 included patients, 12 (57%) were male, and the median (IQR) age was 62.5 (54.0-73.2) years. A total of 19 patients had clear-cell RCC; all tumors were grade 3 or 4, and 3 patients had metastatic disease at enrollment. At a median (range) follow-up of 108.6 (2.0-127.2) months, 1-year RFS was 71.4% (80% CI, 56.6-82.0; 95% CI, 47.2-86.0), meeting the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion based on comparison with the historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7% (P = .09). One-year overall survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3) and cancer-specific survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3). title: Body Composition Metrics and Overall Survival in Head and Neck Cancer Radiotherapy.
abstract: Importance Advancing the prognostication of patients with head and neck cancer who are undergoing radiotherapy may guide clinicians to better individualize support throughout oncologic treatment. Objective To evaluate how automated 3-dimensional soft tissue phenotyping, as extracted from routine computed tomography (CT) scans, provides deeper biological granularity into body composition and mortality risk and examine the prognostic utility of baseline body mass index. Design, setting, and participants This retrospective cohort study evaluated a consecutive sample of patients who were receiving conventionally fractionated definitive-intent radiotherapy for head and neck cancer between January 1, 2014, and December 31, 2024, at a single-center tertiary academic referral center. Cohort filtering was applied to exclude palliative, abbreviated, or nonstandard treatment regimens. Data were analyzed from October 2025 to May 2026. Exposures Baseline body composition metrics, including body mass index and 3-dimensional volumetric soft tissue indices, extracted automatically from pretreatment CT simulation scans using an open-source deep learning segmentation pipeline. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was overall survival. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess the independent prognostic associations of baseline body mass index and volumetric soft tissue indices, controlling for standard clinical confounders. Results The primary clinical cohort comprised 1187 patients (median [range] age, 64.0 [5.0-100.0] years; 323 female individuals [27.2%] and 864 male individuals [72.8%]), with an imaging subcohort of 659 patients (55.5%). While elevated body mass index categories were associated with overall survival (overweight: hazard ratio [HR], 0.70; 95% CI, 0.56-0.89; obesity: HR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.50-0.89), a volumetric analysis revealed that this expansion was disproportionately associated with subcutaneous adiposity gain rather than muscle growth. In the imaging subcohort, elevated skeletal muscle was associated with improved overall survival (HR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.50-0.89; P = .001). Conversely, elevated intermuscular adiposity was independently associated with an increased mortality risk (HR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.03-1.58; P = .02). Conclusions and relevance The results of this cohort study suggest that higher body mass index was associated with improved overall survival. Automated volumetric CT phenotyping revealed that higher skeletal muscle and lower intermuscular adiposity were also associated with improved survival outcomes. This scalable, opportunistic framework may guide pretreatment risk stratification to identify vulnerable patients who may benefit from targeted supportive care.

title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Relapse in Major Depressive Disorder.
abstract: Importance Early identification of patients at high risk of relapse is key to personalized preventive strategies in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, current predictive models do not adequately account for the multimodal factors contributing to MDD relapse and fail to provide clinically meaningful predictions. Objective To predict relapse within 2 years in patients with MDD by using a comprehensive machine learning pipeline that integrates an unprecedented set of multimodal data. Design, setting, and participants This naturalistic longitudinal prognostic study used data from the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study, with baseline assessments collected from October 2014 to May 2019 and follow-up approximately 2 years later, between October 2016 and June 2021. Data analysis was conducted between July 2024 and June 2026. The study was performed at 2 sites in Germany (Marburg and Münster), with participants recruited from psychiatric inpatient and outpatient departments and the general population. Patients meeting diagnostic criteria for current or lifetime MDD without history of neurological or severe somatic conditions were included. Exposure Natural course of illness in patients with MDD. Main outcomes and measures Balanced accuracy (BACC) for binary prediction of relapse vs no relapse during 2-year follow-up served as the primary outcome. Baseline features comprised 9 modalities including clinical and psychometric data, 4 structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging modalities, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome. Results A total of 564 patients with a current or lifetime MDD diagnosis were included (367 female [65.1%]; mean [SD] age, 37.34 [13.38] years). A total of 270 patients relapsed during the 2-year follow-up, while 294 did not. Mean (SD) BACC for the prediction of relapse ranged from 47.21% (5.85%) to 64.43% (6.63%). The best-performing model was solely based on few clinical relapse risk factors, while multimodal data integration did not improve performance. Conclusions and relevance In this prognostic study, the models achieved moderate accuracy, yet the results suggest limited scope for guiding individual-level clinical decision-making. Predictive performance was largely driven by established clinical risk factors, indicating limited incremental value of multimodal measures when assessed at a single time point. Future advances may instead benefit from dynamic modeling approaches that more closely align temporally evolving multimodal markers with longitudinal clinical outcomes.

title: The Added Value of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in Children With Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Presenting as a Clinically Isolated Lesion.
abstract: Background The clinical utility of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in children diagnosed with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) who present with a clinically isolated lesion remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the added value of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in identifying occult lesions and assessing its impact on disease classification and clinical outcomes in this patient population. Methods This retrospective study included children who underwent surgical resection of a clinically isolated lesion, were confirmed to have LCH by histopathology, and received 18 F-FDG PET/CT prior to initiation of systemic therapy. Outcomes including detection of additional lesions, disease reclassification, and progression-free survival were analyzed. Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank test was used to compare progression-free survival between groups. Results A total of 44 children were included (median age 4.29 years; 70.5% male). 18 F-FDG PET/CT identified additional lesions in 24 patients (54.5%), leading to reclassification as single-system multifocal disease in 10 (22.7%) and multisystem disease in 14 (31.8%). Four patients (9.1%) had risk organ involvement. 18 F-FDG PET/CT findings altered the treatment strategy in 54.5% of patients. All 5 relapsed patients belonged to the group with additional lesions (p = 0.044). Conclusion 18 F-FDG PET/CT detected additional lesions in over half of the children diagnosed with LCH presenting as a clinically isolated lesion, resulting in disease reclassification and improved risk stratification. 18 F-FDG PET/CT should be routinely performed in this clinical scenario to ensure accurate staging and appropriate treatment.

title: An X-ray micro-CT protocol enables non-destructive 3D visualization of glandular architecture in archived paraffin-embedded prostate cancer tissue.
abstract: The prostate is organized as a complex glandular network, and prostate cancer is accompanied by architectural changes that cannot always be inferred from two-dimensional (2D) histology. The study of these features in three dimensions (3D) in cancerous tissue is important because glandular features have shown potential value for disease characterization and risk stratification beyond that obtained from individual 2D sections. Large collections of clinically annotated material preserved in paraffin remain an important research source. However, many 3D imaging methods require destructive or labor-intensive preparation, limiting access to valuable material that needs to be re-archived. In this proof-of-concept study, we developed an X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) workflow for direct 3D imaging of archived paraffin-embedded prostate specimens with near-zero sample manipulation. Imaging and denoising parameters were optimized to balance image quality with acquisition time. Paraffin-embedded prostate core punches (n = 5) from five radical prostatectomy specimens were imaged by micro-CT and subsequently processed for histology. Digitized histological sections were aligned with corresponding micro-CT planes for qualitative comparison, while pre-sectioning micro-CT data provided an intact geometric reference for exploratory assessment of histology-associated dimensional changes at the whole-core and glandular-lumen levels. The optimized workflow yielded micro-CT images with discernible glandular morphology and qualitative structural correspondence with matched histological sections. Exploratory measurements suggested modest dimensional change at the whole-core level and greater variability at the lumen level; none of the tested deformation metrics reached conventional statistical significance. Illustrative 3D segmentation presented the glandular epithelium and lumina as spatially continuous structures within a cancer-containing region. These findings support the feasibility of X-ray micro-CT as a non-destructive approach for 3D characterization of prostate glandular architecture directly from paraffin-embedded tissue, providing volumetric context for structures identified on histology while preserving the specimen for subsequent histological assessment.

title: Deep learning-based dose prediction for stereotactic prostate cancer radiotherapy with CyberKnife.
abstract: Background Deep learning-based (DL) approaches have gained interest in predicting dose distributions in radiotherapy of prostate cancer treated with volumetric modulated arc therapy and intensity-modulated radiation therapy. Meanwhile, research on predicting dose distributions in high-precision stereotactic radiotherapy treatments has remained relatively underrepresented. Purpose We aimed to expand the previous studies by developing a DL-based framework for predicting dose distributions for robotic, stereotactic prostate cancer radiotherapy. Methods We harnessed a U-Net-based convolutional neural network for predicting clinically achievable dose distributions based on CT images, delineated structures, and distance information from the planning target volume. A dataset of 462 patients treated with CyberKnife (Accuray Inc.) utilizing an Iris collimator was divided into training (70%, n = 323), validation (10%, n = 46), and test (20%, n = 93) sets. Results In the independent test set, the mean absolute error between the mean doses of predictions and clinical plans was 0.63 Gy for the rectum and 1.04 Gy for the bladder. Conclusions The proposed U-Net-based model demonstrated the ability to learn and reproduce characteristic dose distributions in CyberKnife prostate cancer radiotherapy. The model may provide patient-specific dose estimates for setting initial planning objectives to assist in automating treatment planning and improving inter-planner consistency.

Conclusions

The proposed U-Net-based model demonstrated the ability to learn and reproduce characteristic dose distributions in CyberKnife prostate cancer radiotherapy. The model may provide patient-specific dose estimates for setting initial planning objectives to assist in automating treatment planning and improving inter-planner consistency.

title: Feasibility of multi-energy CT and fat fraction MRI for characterizing active bone marrow response to pelvic external beam radiation therapy.
abstract: Background Pelvic external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), frequently exposes a substantial fraction of active bone marrow (ABM), leading to radiation-induced marrow suppression and associated hematologic toxicity. Accurate delineation and quantitative assessment of ABM are therefore essential to enable marrow-sparing radiotherapy strategies. Purpose To identify and quantify changes in ABM after EBRT using multi-energy CT (MECT) and fat fraction MRI (FFMRI). Methods Patients with gynecological malignancies underwent MECT and FFMRI pre- and post-radiation therapy. ABM was delineated on both imaging modalities using thresholding where ABM was defined as voxels with CT numbers above the mean in MECT-derived virtual non-calcium (VNCa) datasets and voxels with percent fat fraction (%FF) below the mean on the FFMRI. ABM volumes and mean HU/%FF values were evaluated before and after treatment. A Wilcoxon-signed rank test was computed to compare paired MECT versus FFMRI ABM volume percent changes. Changes in ABM as a function of dose were also evaluated. A paired t-test was computed for each dose gradient (significant p < 0.05). Results The average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) between the MECT and FFMRI pre-treatment ABM volumes was 0.57 (range: 0.50-0.68). The mean volumetric change in ABM volume between pre- and post-treatment scans was -37% ± 15% (range -57% to -12%) and -66% ± 27% (range 8% to -94%) for MECT and FFMRI, respectively. All paired patients demonstrated greater ABM volume reduction with FFMRI than with MECT, and this difference was statistically significant (p = 0.0078). ABM changes were observed as a function of dose: A decrease in mean CT numbers and an increase in %FF corresponds to an increase in dose. CT number decreased significantly at doses ≥10 Gy (p ≤ 0.005), while %FF increased significantly across all dose gradients (p ≤ 0.0017), with both metrics showing strong dose‑response behavior at higher doses (p < 10 - 6 ). Conclusions This feasibility study demonstrates the utility of using MECT and FFMRI for delineating ABM in patients receiving pelvic EBRT. These imaging modalities showed good agreement in characterizing ABM volumes changes and radiation-induced marrow suppression. These findings support further investigation of ABM segmentation into the RT-planning workflow to facilitate marrow-sparing strategies.

title: Impact of 4D-CT MIP reconstruction method on iGTV definition: A clinical case report.
abstract: To present a clinical case demonstrating the impact of 4D-CT maximum intensity projection (MIP) reconstruction methodology on internal gross tumor volume (iGTV) definition and to highlight implications for motion management quality assurance. During routine thoracic radiation therapy treatment planning, a discrepancy in tumor extent was identified during physician contouring. The inferior extent of the tumor appeared artificially truncated on the MIP dataset used for target delineation. Further review revealed that the default MIP had been generated from phase-sorted 4D-CT images. A comparison was performed between the phase-sorted MIP and a MIP reconstructed from the original cine images to evaluate differences in motion representation. The phase-sorted MIP under-represented the full tumor motion envelope, most notably in the inferior direction. In contrast, the cine-based MIP demonstrated a more complete representation of tumor extent throughout respiration. This discrepancy was not readily apparent during the routine clinical workflow, and verification of the MIP reconstruction method was not part of the standard QA review process at the time. Differences in MIP reconstruction methodology can impact iGTV definition. Although these differences may be subtle in most cases, clinically meaningful discrepancies may occur, particularly in patients with irregular breathing patterns. This case highlights the importance of awareness and verification of 4D-CT MIP reconstruction methods and supports comprehensive QA across CT simulation, treatment planning, and motion management workflows.

title: Enhancing diagnostic precision for BI-RADS 4a breast nodules: A multimodal AI model integrating ultrasound radiomics, hemodynamic signatures, and clinical profiles.
abstract: Background Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) 4a nodules represent a diagnostic dilemma, with a malignancy rate ranging from 2% to 10%. The majority of these nodules prove benign after biopsy, leading to unnecessary invasive procedures, patient anxiety, and healthcare costs. Current clinical practice lacks a reliable, noninvasive tool to accurately distinguish benign from malignant BI-RADS 4a lesions. Emerging evidence suggests that integrating multiparametric ultrasound data with clinical factors through artificial intelligence may improve diagnostic precision, but a validated multimodal model specifically for this ambiguous category is lacking. Purpose To develop and validate a multimodal artificial intelligence model that integrates ultrasound radiomics, hemodynamic features, and clinical data for the accurate differentiation of benign and malignant BI-RADS 4a breast nodules, with the ultimate goal of supporting clinical decisionmaking and safely reducing unnecessary biopsies. Methods This prospective, multicenter study enrolled 350 pathologically confirmed BI-RADS 4a nodules from 331 patients in one tertiary hospital and two secondary hospitals. Clinical data, grayscale ultrasound images, and hemodynamic parameters were collected for each nodule. Radiomics features were extracted from the ultrasound images. A multimodal fusion model was constructed using the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) algorithm following feature selection via Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression. The model was developed and hyperparameter-tuned on a training set (n = 260) using nested cross-validation and was evaluated on a temporally independent test set (n = 90). Model interpretability was enhanced using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results On the independent test set, the multimodal LightGBM model demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.91-0.99), with a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 81.5%-100%) and a specificity of 86.1% (95% CI: 75.8%-93.1%). Its performance was significantly superior to baseline classifiers including Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest (all p < 0.05). SHAP analysis identified wavelet-transformed texture features, the presence of a penetrating vessel, and BRCA mutation status as the top predictors of malignancy. Applying this model could have potentially avoided 32.4% (24/74) of unnecessary biopsies on benign nodules while maintaining perfect sensitivity. Conclusion A multimodal AI model based on LightGBM can accurately differentiate benign and malignant BI-RADS 4a breast nodules. It shows significant potential as a clinical decision-support tool to reduce unnecessary biopsies without compromising sensitivity, enabling more precise management for this challenging patient population.

title: Evaluation of registration accuracy using short-arc cone-beam computed tomography for image-guided radiotherapy in breast cancer.
abstract: Background Image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enables highly accurate imaging registration; however, increased radiation exposure remains a concern. Recently, short-arc CBCT (SA-CBCT), which reduces projection data and reconstructs images, has become available. Although previous studies have shown that image quality deteriorates when projection data are reduced, no study has directly evaluated the clinical usefulness of SA-CBCT or its effect on registration accuracy. Purpose We verified the registration accuracy of SA-CBCT in breast tangential irradiation using an anthropomorphic phantom and clinical data, and examined its clinical feasibility compared with the commonly used 200° scan. Methods An anthropomorphic phantom was placed on the treatment bed, and CT and CBCT images acquired during treatment planning were aligned. Bed movement was measured for both conventional CBCT and SA-CBCT images. The difference between the two measurements was quantified as N, defined as the norm of the vector difference between CBCT and SA-CBCT registration shifts, to evaluate registration accuracy. The acquisition angle was varied to assess the effects of central and total angles. In the clinical study, registration data from 30 consecutive patients who underwent whole-breast irradiation were analyzed. Data were reconstructed by changing the acquisition angle from 200° to 120°, and N was calculated as in the phantom experiment. Results In the phantom experiment, N was within 0.15 mm (3-axis) and 0.55 mm (6-axis) when the acquisition angle was reduced to 120°. In clinical data, the average N was 0.64 mm in 3-axis registration (84.7% within 1 mm) and 0.85 mm in 6-axis registration (71.3% within 1 mm). Even with a 120° acquisition angle, the body contour and chest wall edges were sufficiently preserved. Conclusions SA-CBCT maintained adequate registration accuracy in breast tangential irradiation. These findings suggest its clinical applicability with appropriate acquisition angle settings.

title: A hybrid deep learning framework for automated treatment planning in cervical cancer radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Radiation therapy treatment planning is a time-consuming trial-and-error process, and the plan quality is heavily dependent on planners' experiences, resulting in a strong demand for automated planning methods that can rapidly generate uniformly high-quality plans. Purpose This study aimed to develop a hybrid automated deep learning-based plan optimization (HALO) framework, integrating deep learning fluence prediction and optimization, multileaf collimator (MLC) sequencing, and GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo dose computation. HALO was designed to ensure robust plan generation for cervical cancer intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). Methods The proposed HALO framework incorporated several functional modules. First, a dose-guided Fluence Prediction Network (DG-FPN) was developed. A total of 120 cervical cancer clinical IMRT plans were collected to train the DG-FPN, of which 90 plans were assigned for training, 10 for validation, and 20 for testing. The neural network took patients' computed tomography (CT) anatomy as input and predicted the 3D dose distribution and fluence maps. Next, the predicted fluence maps were further optimized to meet dose-volume constraints (DVCs), and then the refined fluence maps were converted into deliverable segments using an MLC sequencing algorithm. Finally, dose calculation was performed using a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo engine. The 20 patients in the testing set were used to evaluate the HALO method, and the plan deliverability was validated by patient-specific IMRT Quality Assurance (QA). Results The DG-FPN achieved superior fluence prediction accuracy compared to previous work, with a median mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.055 and a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.94. The automated framework generated high-quality plans and reduced dose to adjacent OARs, with V 50Gy decreased from 46.5 ± 5.0% to 41.5 ± 4.8% (p = 0.008)for bladder, V 35Gy decreased from 31.5 ± 8.2% to 29.2 ± 7.5% (p = 0.024) for small intestine, while preserving PTV homogeneity and conformity. Importantly, the entire treatment planning time was within 3 minutes, with fluence optimization time decreased by an average of 82.6% after using deep learning prediction. The mean gamma passing rate under the 2%/2 mm criterion for the patient-specific IMRT QA achieved 97.37 ± 1.01%. Conclusions This study demonstrated the clinical feasibility of the proposed HALO framework for cervical cancer radiotherapy in producing high-quality and deliverable IMRT plans. The proposed automated paradigm can serve as a stand-alone platform for treatment planning.

title: Maskless head and neck radiotherapy using surface-guided radiation therapy: initial clinical feasibility of real-time setup, intrafraction monitoring, and automatic beam-hold.
abstract: Background Thermoplastic immobilization remains standard for head and neck radiation therapy, but rigid face masks may produce clinically meaningful anxiety, claustrophobia, and treatment intolerance in some patients. Surface-guided radiation therapy (SGRT) provides non-ionizing surface setup guidance and continuous intrafraction motion monitoring, potentially enabling reduced-immobilization treatment approaches. Purpose To describe and initially evaluate the clinical feasibility of a thermoplastic-maskless head and neck radiation therapy workflow using a posterior dorsal shell, SGRT-guided setup, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) verification, and real-time intrafraction monitoring with automatic beam-hold. Methods Ten patients with head and neck cancer were treated without a thermoplastic face mask. Patients were positioned in a posterior dorsal shell. Daily setup began with SGRT followed by CBCT verification and couch correction. During delivery, SGRT (AlignRT v6.3, Vision RT, London, UK) monitored head position in six degrees of freedom (6DoF); automatic beam-hold was triggered when translational displacement exceeded 2 mm or rotational displacement exceeded 2°. Post-treatment CBCT and SGRT log files were reviewed for every fraction to characterize residual displacement, threshold events, and repositioning. Intrafraction motion and residual displacement were summarized as medians with interquartile range (IQR). Results Across 330 delivered fractions, sgrt-recorded intrafraction motion was small:: per-axis signed real-time deltas had a median [IQR] of 0.10 mm [-0.15, 0.30] translationally and 0.10° [-0.05, 0.20] rotationally. No fraction had a mean real-time delta exceeding the ± 2 mm/ ± 2° tolerance, and automatic beam-hold interruptions occurred in approximately 2% of fractions (7 of 330); no fraction was abandoned. Per-axis post-treatment CBCT residuals were -0.01 mm [-0.04, 0.05] translationally and 0.15° [-0.40, 0.55] rotationally. All patients completed the maskless course; 3 of 10 had previously declined or been unable to tolerate mask-based treatment, and all reported the maskless workflow to be well tolerated on an end-of-course questionnaire. Conclusions A thermoplastic-maskless head and neck workflow using SGRT, CBCT verification, predefined beam-hold thresholds, and dorsal shell support was feasible in this initial 10-patient experience, maintaining small observed intrafraction motion while directly addressing mask intolerance. Larger prospective evaluation with validated patient-reported outcomes, dosimetric analysis, and multi-institutional QA is warranted.
