title: Preoperative 7 T 3D Meniscal T2* Mapping Correlates With Postoperative Extrusion After Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear Repair.
abstract: Medial meniscus posterior root tear (MMPRT) repairs stabilize root attachment and yield improved clinical outcomes, yet many patients develop persistent meniscal extrusion and osteoarthritis. This study evaluates menisci in MMPRT patients using 3D T2* mapping and assesses T2* correlation with medial meniscal extrusion. Patients underwent 7 T knee MRI before root tear repair and again at 6-month postoperative follow-up. Age- and gender-matched controls were scanned once. The protocol included clinical turbo-spin-echo sequences and a quantitative 3D GRE sequence, used to calculate T2* mapping of the menisci. Pre- and postrepair meniscal extrusion was measured on coronal T2-weighted images by two independent radiologists. Twenty-five patients (mean age 53 ± 8 years) and nine controls (51 ± 11 years) were included. Repairs were intact on follow-up MRI in all patients. T2* values were significantly elevated in patients both pre- and postrepair compared with controls across medial and lateral meniscal subregions. Medial meniscal extrusion increased from 3.7 ± 1.1 mm at baseline to 4.9 ± 1.5 mm (p = 0.002), postoperatively. Prerepair meniscal T2* strongly correlated with postrepair extrusion (ρ = 0.765; p < 0.001). High-resolution 3D T2* mapping at 7 T revealed persistently elevated T2* values after MMPRT repair, consistent with ongoing collagen fiber disorganization. Prerepair T2* values were strongly correlated with early postrepair meniscal extrusion despite MRI-intact repairs, indicating that preoperative tissue quality is associated with postoperative outcomes. These findings support quantitative T2* mapping as a prognostic imaging biomarker that complements conventional morphologic MRI in the evaluation of MMPRTs.

title: Circumferential Meniscal Extrusion Mapping Using Radial Multiplanar Reconstructions.
abstract: Meniscal extrusion is a marker of meniscal dysfunction and has been associated with osteoarthritis progression. Assessment is typically performed on a single coronal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slice, but this method may miss the location of maximal circumferential displacement. We developed an extrusion mapping technique using radially oriented multiplanar reconstruction (rMPR) images from high-resolution 3D MRI to enable circumferential meniscal position measurements perpendicular to the tibial margin. Extrusion was measured by three independent readers on rMPR images generated from non-fat-saturated 3D fast spin-echo MRI in 20 patients stratified by meniscal tear and extrusion status. Intrareader and interreader measurement variabilities were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), 95% repeatability coefficient (RC; intrareader), and 95% reproducibility coefficient (RDC; interreader). Corresponding rMPR and standard 2D coronal midbody extrusion measurements were compared. Intrareader variability was low, with a mean within-meniscus within-angle standard deviation (SD) of 0.2 mm and mean RC of 0.6 mm. Interreader variability was also low, with a mean within-meniscus within-angle SD of 0.5 mm and mean RDC of 1.4 mm. At the midbody, there was 98% concordance for extrusion classification between rMPR and 2D coronal measurements within the interreader RDC (1.4 mm). Exploratory regional analysis suggested different extrusion patterns between medial and lateral menisci and between torn and intact menisci. These findings suggest that circumferential meniscal extrusion mapping using rMPR images from 3D knee MRI is feasible, with low intrareader and interreader measurement variabilities. This framework enables regional characterization of meniscal displacement and should support future investigations of meniscus-osteoarthritis relationships. STATEMENT OF CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Meniscus extrusion circumferential mapping using radially oriented multiplanar reconstruction images is feasible and consistent across readers and allows a more complete assessment of meniscal position, which may be valuable for further investigation of meniscal injury and osteoarthritis.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus infection mimicking very early onset inflammatory bowel disease.
abstract: Very early onset inflammatory bowel disease (VEO-IBD), defined as diagnosis before 6 years of age, is often associated with immune dysregulation and monogenic etiologies; however, infectious mimics may be overlooked in low-prevalence regions. We report a 4-year-old male with poor weight gain, intermittent diarrhea, elevated fecal calprotectin, and persistently elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Endoscopy showed diffuse friable colonic mucosa, and biopsies demonstrated focal active colitis with mild crypt distortion. He was diagnosed with VEO-IBD and treated with mesalamine, infliximab, adalimumab, and upadacitinib, with incomplete response. At age 7, he was hospitalized with fever, cytopenias, and pulmonary infiltrates; human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) testing was positive, with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus viremia. After discontinuing immunosuppression and initiating antiretroviral therapy, gastrointestinal symptoms and inflammatory markers improved. HIV-associated colitis can closely mimic VEO-IBD, and progressive lymphopenia should prompt evaluation for secondary immunodeficiency.

title: Defining the Clinical Indication for Real-Time Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ultrasound in Breast Lesions with Low Suspicion of Malignancy.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether real-time artificial intelligence (AI) breast ultrasound (US) can identify a subgroup of breast imaging reporting and data system (BI-RADS) category 4A lesions without suspicious mammographic (MMG) findings in whom unnecessary biopsy may be safely avoided. Methods This retrospective analysis of single-center biopsy registry included 641 consecutive US BI-RADS 4A lesions that underwent vacuum-assisted breast biopsy. Before conducting biopsy, the lesions were reassessed using a real-time AI US system (CadAI-B®), and MMG findings were classified as suspicious or non-suspicious based on formal reports. Seven prespecified biopsy-decision strategies were evaluated, including 3 AI-only strategies, 3 mammography-gated AI strategies, and the current standard strategy of biopsy all BI-RADS 4A lesions. The primary outcomes were biopsy reduction rate, missed cancers, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy, with final pathology as the reference standard. Results Among 641 cases of US BI-RADS 4A lesions, 26 cases of malignancies (4.1%) were identified, including 14 cases of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), 11 cases of invasive ductal carcinomas, and 1 case of apocrine carcinoma. AI reassigned 289 cases of lesions (45.1%) to BI-RADS categories 1-3. AI-only biopsy-deferral strategies missed 30.8% and 38.5% of malignancies when biopsy was deferred for AI BI-RADS ≤2 and ≤3 lesions, respectively, with DCIS accounting for most missed cancers. In contrast, among lesions without suspicious MMG findings, no malignancies were observed in AI BI-RADS 1-3 lesions. The sequential strategy of deferring biopsy only for lesions with AI BI-RADS ≤3 and non-suspicious MMG findings reduced biopsies by 43.5% (279/641) while maintaining 100.0% sensitivity (95% CI, 87.1-100.0%) and increasing specificity to 45.4% (95% CI, 41.4-49.4%). Conclusion Real-time AI breast US alone could not safely support biopsy deferral in US BI-RADS 4A lesions. However, after suspicious MMG findings had been excluded, AI identified a low-risk subgroup in whom unnecessary biopsy could be substantially reduced without compromising cancer detection. These findings suggest that the clinical utility of real-time AI breast US lies in patients without suspicious MMG findings. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted before clinical implementation.

title: Value of Multimodal Ultrasound Imaging With Super-Resolution in the Differential Diagnosis of Benign and Malignant Superficial Lymph Nodes: A Dual-Center Prospective Study.
abstract: Objectives Accurate differential diagnosis of benign and malignant superficial lymph nodes (LNs) is critical for clinical management. The objectives of this study were to explore the feasibility and clinical value of super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) in the differential diagnosis of superficial lymphadenopathy and to establish and validate a multimodal ultrasound diagnostic model based on conventional ultrasound (US), contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), and SRUS, so as to improve the accuracy of distinguishing benign from malignant superficial LNs in clinical practice. Methods A total of 200 LNs from 165 patients with superficial lymphadenectasis were prospectively enrolled from two medical centers. All patients underwent conventional US, CEUS, and SRUS imaging. Predictive models were constructed based on the conventional US, CEUS, and SRUS features in the training cohort, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were calculated to evaluate their predictive performance in the external validation cohort. Results The training cohort comprised 117 patients with a total of 140 LNs including 46 benign and 94 malignant lesions. The validation cohort included 48 patients with 60 LNs in total, with 21 benign and 39 malignant lesions. Among the models constructed based on the training cohort, the SRUS model exhibited significantly superior diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.822) to the conventional US and CEUS models (P < .05). title: ACR TI-RADS Modified by CEUS Features and Nodule Location for Diagnosis and Biopsy Decision in Thyroid Nodules of TR4 or Higher.
abstract: Objectives To develop a modified American College of Radiology (ACR) thyroid imaging, reporting and data system (TI-RADS) incorporating contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) features and nodule location to improve diagnostic performance and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) recommendations for ACR TR4 or higher thyroid nodules. Methods This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent ultrasound and CEUS at 3 hospitals between June 2024 and January 2026. CEUS and location features were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression to construct the modified system. Diagnostic performance and biopsy recommendation efficiency were compared with ACR TI-RADS. Results Four hundred and eight patients with 442 nodules were included. Independent predictors included enhancement intensity, enhancement direction, ring enhancement, enhancement area and nodule location. In the training set (n = 334), the modified system achieved higher AUC and sensitivity than ACR TI-RADS (AUC: 0.90 [95% CI: 0.86-0.93] versus 0.75 [95% CI: 0.71-0.79]; sensitivity: 88.5% versus 60.3%; p < .01), higher accuracy of malignant nodule biopsies (AMB: 67.1% versus 49.4%), lower unnecessary biopsy rate (UBR: 32.9% versus 50.6%), and lower biopsy rate of benign nodules (BRB: 20.8% versus 31.2%), with no unsafe downgrading. Similar results were observed in the temporal validation set (n = 108): AUC 0.95 (95% CI: 0.90-0.99) versus 0.73 (95% CI: 0.66-0.79); sensitivity 87.0% versus 49.3%; AMB 83.3% versus 53.3%; UBR 16.7% versus 46.7%, and BRB 5.1% versus 17.9%. Conclusions A modified ACR TI-RADS integrating CEUS features and nodule location improved diagnostic performance and FNA recommendations for ACR TR4 or higher nodules. Pending external validation, this system may provide a practical approach for refining risk stratification and reducing unnecessary biopsies.

title: Multiparametric Ultrasound in Budd-Chiari Syndrome: From Venous Outflow Obstruction to Microcirculatory Dysfunction.
abstract: Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) is a rare and potentially severe disorder of hepatic venous outflow with a heterogeneous anatomical and etiological spectrum. Obstruction may range from focal or segmental involvement of a single hepatic vein to multifocal hepatic venous disease with inferior vena cava (IVC) involvement. Although BCS is traditionally diagnosed by demonstrating macroscopic venous obstruction, its clinical severity also depends on the resulting changes in sinusoidal pressure, hepatic perfusion, collateral circulation, and the intrahepatic microcirculation. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), although less common than myeloproliferative neoplasms as an underlying cause of BCS, represents a particularly severe prothrombotic model in which macrovascular thrombosis may coexist with systemic vascular and microcirculatory abnormalities. The purpose of the study is to provide a pathophysiology-oriented review of BCS, with emphasis on the relationship between hepatic venous outflow obstruction, altered hepatic hemodynamics, tissue perfusion, microcirculatory dysfunction, and the complementary role of conventional and advanced imaging techniques, using PNH as a model of severe thrombotic BCS. A narrative literature review was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE and related biomedical databases for publications from January 2000 to March 2026, supplemented by relevant earlier landmark studies. Literature addressing the etiology and pathophysiology of BCS, PNH-associated thrombosis, hepatic hemodynamics, conventional and advanced ultrasound techniques, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was reviewed. Particular attention was given to Doppler ultrasound, contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), parametric perfusion imaging, microvascular flow imaging, and elastography. BCS results from a broad spectrum of primary and secondary causes, including myeloproliferative neoplasms, PNH, inherited and acquired thrombophilia, malignancy, trauma, and iatrogenic conditions. The anatomical extent and duration of venous obstruction determine the degree of sinusoidal hypertension, hepatic congestion, redistribution of portal and arterial flow, and development of intrahepatic collateral pathways. Conventional Doppler ultrasound remains the foundation of diagnosis and provides assessment of venous patency, the extent of obstruction, waveform abnormalities, portal and arterial hemodynamics, and collateral circulation. CEUS and parametric perfusion imaging provide complementary information regarding regional and temporal hepatic perfusion, while microvascular flow imaging may demonstrate slow residual flow and small collateral pathways not readily visualized with conventional Doppler. Elastography provides additional information regarding congestion-related tissue stiffness and chronic remodeling. CT and MRI remain essential for comprehensive anatomical characterization, identification of secondary causes, assessment of parenchymal complications, and treatment planning. BCS should be regarded as a dynamic disorder of hepatic circulation rather than solely as an anatomical abnormality of the hepatic veins or IVC. A multiparametric imaging approach integrating morphology, macrovascular hemodynamics, tissue perfusion, microvascular flow, and tissue mechanics may provide a more comprehensive assessment of disease phenotype and treatment response than assessment of venous patency alone. PNH provides a particularly informative model for understanding the interaction between macrovascular thrombosis and microcirculatory dysfunction. However, advanced ultrasound techniques remain complementary and require further prospective validation, standardization, and correlation with hemodynamic measurements, hepatic functional reserve, and clinical outcomes.

title: Preoperative varus ≥10° does not compromise outcome after medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, whereas postoperative joint-line convergence angle and insert thickness influence functional results: A matched-pair analysis.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate functional outcomes and implant survival following medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) in patients with anteromedial osteoarthritis and preoperative varus deformity ≥10° and to identify postoperative alignment thresholds that optimize outcomes. Methods Patients with preoperative varus ≥10° who underwent medial mobile-bearing UKA were retrospectively analysed and matched 1:1 to knees with preoperative varus <10°, yielding 132 pairs (264 knees) with similar baseline characteristics. Primary outcomes were revision rates and the Oxford Knee Score (OKS). Full-length standing radiographs were used to measure the hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), joint-line convergence angle (JLCA), extra-articular deformity (EAD), mechanical medial proximal tibial angle (mMPTA), mechanical lateral distal femoral angle (mLDFA) and joint-line obliquity (JLO) and determine functional knee phenotypes. Univariate curve-adjusted regression assessed the influence of alignment on OKS, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis defined the alignment range within which the Patient-Acceptable Symptomatic State (PASS) was achieved. Results At a mean follow-up of 10.1 ± 3.3 years, OKS did not differ between groups (40.6 ± 8.0 vs. 38.8 ± 5.7, n.s.), nor did revision-free survival (92.3% vs. 90.2% at 10 years, p = 0.618). In knees with preoperative varus ≥10°, postoperative JLCA correlated with OKS (R 2 = 0.43, p < 0.001), whereas HKA, EAD, mMPTA, mLDFA and JLO showed no association (p > 0.05). JLCA outside 0°-5° varus yielded inferior OKS (35.6 ± 11.0 vs. 42.4 ± 6.2, p = 0.022) and lower PASS achievement (33% vs. 70%, p = 0.011). Insert thickness ≥7 mm was associated with lower OKS (32.1 ± 12.1 vs. 41.2 ± 5.9, p = 0.004) and reduced PASS (30% vs. 81%, p = 0.046). Conclusions Medial UKA in knees with preoperative varus deformity ≥10° achieved functional outcomes and implant survival comparable to matched knees with varus <10°, provided postoperative JLCA is restored to 0°-5° varus and excessive insert thickness is avoided. Intraoperative insert upsizing should prompt reassessment for ligamentous insufficiency or compartment overstuffing. Level of evidence Level III.

title: Greater three-dimensional cam burden and superolateral location are associated with end-stage hip osteoarthritis: A retrospective comparative study.
abstract: Purpose Cam-type femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a recognised structural contributor to primary hip osteoarthritis (OA), yet many cam-positive hips do not progress to radiographic joint failure. This study aimed to compare three-dimensional cam morphology and lesion location between cam-positive hips with end-stage primary osteoarthritis and cam-positive, non-arthritic hips in an elderly fracture cohort. Methods Hospital records and imaging archives from January 2020 to January 2026 were retrospectively reviewed at a single centre. The OA group comprised patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty for primary OA, and the fracture group comprised patients aged ≥ 65 years treated for intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric femoral fractures without radiographic OA. Cam morphology was characterised using radial CT-based alpha angle, three-dimensional cam volume, cam/head volume ratio, and clock-face-based lesion location. Group comparisons, receiver operating characteristic analyses, correlation testing, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Results A total of 438 cam-positive hips were included (126 OA and 312 fracture). OA hips demonstrated higher alpha angles (72.44° ± 5.94° vs. 62.45° ± 5.07°), larger cam volumes (5274.77 ± 1353.26 mm 3 vs. 3215.20 ± 1524.84 mm 3 ), higher cam/head ratios (8.61% ± 2.02% vs. 6.35% ± 1.97%), and more superolateral lesions (52.4% vs. 36.2% anterior in the fracture group) (all p < 0.001). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses identified cohort-specific discriminatory values of 66° for alpha angle (AUC, 0.884), 4421 mm 3 for cam volume (AUC, 0.839), and 6.4% for the cam-to-head volume ratio (AUC, 0.791). In multivariable analyses using continuous morphology measures, higher alpha angle, greater cam volume, higher cam-to-head volume ratio, and superolateral lesion location were associated with end-stage OA-group membership. Conclusions Compared with non-arthritic cam-positive hips in an elderly fracture cohort, end-stage primary OA hips had greater three-dimensional cam burden, with lesions more often located superolaterally. These retrospective associations do not establish longitudinal progression, causality, or individual prognosis. Study design Retrospective comparative study. Level of evidence Level III, study of a non-consecutive patients, study of diagnostic test.

title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
abstract: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Double-level osteotomy versus high tibial osteotomy for varus malalignment of the knee: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Purpose To compare double-level osteotomy (DLO) with high tibial osteotomy (HTO) for varus knee malalignment across patient-reported, radiographic, operative and complication outcomes. Methods PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 15 May 2026 for comparative DLO versus HTO studies. Outcomes were pooled with a random-effects model as mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), with absolute values for each arm. The primary outcome was joint-line obliquity (JLO). Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, one cohort per centre, comparable indications) were post hoc. Results Nine observational studies (805 knees; 306 DLO, 499 HTO) were included. At a mean follow-up of 3 years, postoperative JLO was lower after DLO than after HTO (four studies; 1.6° vs. 5.9°; MD: -4.14°, 95%CI: -5.22, -3.06; I 2 = 76%). DLO produced a lower MPTA (seven studies; 91.3° vs. 95.4°; MD: -4.10°, 95%CI: -5.30, -2.90), LDFA (four studies; 86.0° vs. 90.2°; MD: -4.04°, 95%CI: -4.49, -3.58) and mLDFA (two studies; 85.6° vs. 89.0°; MD: -3.37°, 95%CI: -4.16, -2.58). The hip-knee-ankle angle difference was small (five studies; MD: -0.96°, 95%CI: -1.83, -0.09) and not robust in sensitivity analyses. No difference was demonstrated for joint-line convergence angle, posterior tibial slope, any KOOS subscale, KSS scores or time to return to sport. Operative time was longer with DLO (two studies; 137 vs. 91 min; MD: 42.9, 95%CI: 25.7, 60.2). Intraoperative hinge fracture was less frequent with DLO (three studies; 14.0% vs. 34.6%; RR: 0.41, 95%CI: 0.23, 0.73). No nonunion was reported. Conclusions At 3 years, no significant difference in patient-reported or functional outcomes was demonstrated between DLO and HTO. DLO achieved correction with less JLO and fewer hinge fractures, at the cost of a longer operation. Because DLO was often selected for bifocal or larger deformities, the radiographic differences partly reflect the indication. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation. Level of evidence Level I.

Intraoperative hinge fracture was less frequent with DLO (three studies; 14.0% vs. 34.6%; RR: 0.41, 95%CI: 0.23, 0.73). No nonunion was reported.

Conclusions

At 3 years, no significant difference in patient-reported or functional outcomes was demonstrated between DLO and HTO. DLO achieved correction with less JLO and fewer hinge fractures, at the cost of a longer operation. Because DLO was often selected for bifocal or larger deformities, the radiographic differences partly reflect the indication. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation.

Level of evidence

Level I.

title: Outcomes of Osseous Microvascular Midface Reconstruction: Does Union Matter?
abstract: Objective(s) To assess rates of bony union and their correlation with postoperative complications following osseous orbitomaxillary microvascular reconstruction. Methods A retrospective review was performed of patients who underwent orbitozygomaticomaxillary reconstruction with composite osseous free flaps at an academic medical center from 2011 to 2024. Demographics, intraoperative variables, and postoperative outcomes were collected. Univariable and multivariable regression analyses were conducted to evaluate factors associated with bony union. Results Fifty-nine patients were identified, with a mean follow-up of 3.53 years. Most subjects underwent maxillary reconstruction following oncologic resection (72.9%). The predominant flap used was the fibula free flap (78.0%), followed by the osteocutaneous radial forearm flap (16.9%). Complication rates included hardware extrusion (25.4%), fistula formation (40.7%), and bone exposure (15.3%). The rate of complete bony union was 50.0%, with partial and nonunion rates of 13.3% and 37.7%, respectively. Nonunion was more likely among patients with fistula formation (OR 4.29, p = 0.038) and those who underwent subsequent free flap (OR 8.46, p = 0.008). Multivariable regression found nonunion was associated with increasing number of sites of possible osteosynthesis (OR 36.8, p = 0.007), use of Virtual Surgical Planning (VSP) (OR 100.5, p = 0.045), and postoperative radiation therapy (OR 13.8, p = 0.032). Age, ASA class, surgeon, flap type, use of locking versus non-locking plates, ischemia time, and time from surgery to CT were not associated with nonunion. Conclusion Nonunion occurred in approximately one third of cases and was associated with increasing sites of possible osteosynthesis, use of VSP, adjuvant radiation, fistula formation, and subsequent free flap. Level of evidence: 4

title: Confocal Ex Vivo Margin Assessment in Transoral Laser Cordectomy: A Pilot Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
abstract: Objectives Margin assessment in transoral laser microsurgery (TLM) for glottic squamous cell carcinoma is challenging due to specimen size, fragmentation, and artifacts. This study evaluated the feasibility and preliminary diagnostic performance of the Histolog Scanner, an ultra-fast ex vivo confocal microscopy system, for intraoperative margin assessment in TLM cordectomy. Methods This prospective pilot study evaluated adult patients undergoing TLM cordectomy for glottic squamous cell carcinoma. Five predefined margins per specimen (anterior, posterior, superior, inferior, deep) were evaluated using Histolog Scanner and compared with conventional hematoxylin and eosin histopathology, used as the reference standard. Concordance, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and diagnostic accuracy were assessed. Results Nineteen patients were included, yielding to 95 evaluable margins. Overall concordance between Histolog Scanner and histopathology was 92.6% (88/95 margins). The scanner identified 12 true-positive, 76 true-negative, five false-positive, and two false-negative margins. Sensitivity was 85.7% (95% CI: 57.2-98.2), specificity 93.8% (95% CI: 86.2-98.0), positive predictive value 70.6% (95% CI: 44.0-89.7), negative predictive value 97.4% (95% CI: 91.0-99.7), and accuracy 92.6% (95% CI: 85.4-97.0). Agreement was substantial (Cohen's kappa = 0.73). Mean acquisition time was 13 min per specimen. Conclusion The Histolog Scanner is a feasible, rapid intraoperative screening tool with high specificity and excellent negative predictive value for ruling out involved margins in TLM cordectomy. It serves as an intraoperative adjunct rather than a replacement for definitive histopathology, which remains essential. Larger multicenter studies are required before widespread clinical setting implementation. Level of evidence: 3

title: Intraoperative Bone Marrow Frozen Sections Reduce Positive Final Margins in Mandibulectomy.
abstract: Objectives To assess the impact of intraoperative bone marrow frozen section (IBMFS) use on final margin status and survival outcomes in patients undergoing mandibulectomy for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and non-SCC neoplasms. Methods A single-center retrospective cohort study was performed of patients undergoing segmental or marginal mandibulectomy for benign or malignant neoplasms between 2009 and 2025. The medical record was reviewed for demographic data, histopathologic disease features, treatment, and outcomes. Univariable and multivariable Cox regression analyses were used to evaluate associations between IBMFS and recurrence-free and overall survival among patients with SCC. Results Of 235 cases, IBMFS were performed in 80.4%. IBMFS analysis was associated with reduced rates of positive final bone margins (1.1% vs. 8.7%, p = 0.014) and overall positive margins (7.9% vs. 19.6%, p = 0.029). Positive IBMFS rate was higher among non-SCC neoplasms than SCC (23.5% vs. 3.5%, p = 0.007), with no significant difference in rate of final positive margins. IBMFS results demonstrated 90.0% sensitivity, 99.4% specificity, and 98.9% concordance with final histopathology. Among SCC patients, IBMFS use was not significantly associated with recurrence-free survival (aHR 0.671, p = 0.320) or overall survival (aHR 0.967, p = 0.923); only nodal disease and age were significantly associated with survival. Conclusions In this retrospective single-center cohort, IBMFS use was associated with improved final margin control across tumor types, including non-SCC neoplasms. Although no survival benefit was demonstrated, its association with margin clearance suggests that IBMFS may be a useful intraoperative adjunct in mandibulectomy for head and neck neoplasms. Level of evidence: 3

title: Early Oral Gastrografin Followed by Immediate CT for Precise Leak Localization and Surgical Planning After Total Laryngectomy.
abstract: Purpose Pharyngocutaneous fistula (PCF) is the most common and clinically significant complication following total laryngectomy, often leading to delayed recovery and increased morbidity. Accurate and early detection of pharyngeal leak is critical; however, conventional imaging modalities such as contrast swallow studies and computed tomography (CT) have limitations in precise anatomical localization. Materials and methods This retrospective cohort study included 117 patients who underwent total laryngectomy between January 2020 and December 2025. Patients were divided into two groups according to the postoperative imaging protocol: Gastrografin swallow followed by immediate CT (Gastrografin-CT group, n = 22) and conventional imaging ( n = 95). Leak localization was assessed using a four-point ordinal scale, and surgically actionable localization was defined as a score ≥ 2. Clinical outcomes and impact on management were also evaluated. Results The Gastrografin-CT protocol demonstrated significantly improved leak localization compared with conventional imaging (mean localization score: 3.00 ± 0.00 vs. 1.62 ± 0.83, p = 0.01). Surgically actionable localization was achieved in all patients in the Gastrografin-CT group compared with 51.2% in the conventional group ( p = 0.03). Leaks were identified on initial imaging in 100% of patients in the Gastrografin-CT group versus 82.9% in the conventional group. Although clinical outcomes, including time to oral feeding, complication rates, and hospital stay, did not significantly differ, the Gastrografin-CT protocol provided more precise anatomical delineation, facilitating targeted surgical planning. Conclusion Performing CT immediately after an oral Gastrografin swallow significantly improves anatomical localization of pharyngeal leaks following total laryngectomy. By integrating leak detection and anatomical delineation in a single imaging session, this protocol enhances surgical decision-making and may serve as a practical adjunct for postoperative evaluation and management of PCF. Level of evidence 3.

title: Beyond the Surface: AI-Assisted Basal Cell Carcinoma Detection via Optical Coherence Tomography.
abstract: Objectives To determine whether integrating an artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support system (VivoAID) into optical coherence tomography (OCT) interpretation improves diagnostic accuracy and efficiency for novice users evaluating basal cell carcinomas (BCCs). Methods Two dermatology research fellows completed a structured OCT training module for BCC identification using the VivoSight Dx system. Each independently reviewed 45 de-identified OCT scans (31 BCC-positive and 14 BCC-negative, negative ones included squamous cell carcinomas, keratoacanthomas, actinic keratoses and scar tissue), with ground truth established by expert clinical interpretation and histopathology, in two sessions: one unassisted and one AI-assisted. Session order was counterbalanced between learners, and scans were re-randomized for AI sessions. In unassisted sessions, learners manually classified scans; in AI-assisted sessions, they reviewed AI-annotated scans, recorded agreement/disagreement, and noted additional findings. Time-to-decision per scan was measured. A linear mixed-effects model in SAS assessed the effect of AI on decision time while accounting for scan difficulty. Results Without AI, correct BCC identification was 62% for Learner 1% and 64% for Learner 2 (combined 63%). With AI assistance, accuracy increased to 78% and 76%, respectively (combined 77%), reflecting relative improvements of 25% and 17% (combined +21%). Mean decision time decreased from 45 to 28 s for Learner 1 and from 35 to 22 s for Learner 2, yielding a combined reduction from 40 to 25 s (~38% faster). AI use significantly reduced decision time by an average of 15.1 s per image (p < 0.0001). AI standalone accuracy versus expert opinion was 64%, comparable to novice baseline performance. Conclusions AI-enhanced OCT with VivoAID significantly improved novice users' diagnostic accuracy and efficiency, despite AI performance alone being similar to baseline novice interpretation. These data support VivoAID's role as a decision-support and potential educational tool in dermatology. Findings are limited by small sample size, single-institution design, and repeated review of the same scans. Trial registration None.

title: Colorectal Cancer: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Signaling Pathways, Clinical Features, Screening, Diagnosis, and Management.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality worldwide and is increasingly characterized by two converging realities: a substantial global burden and a rising incidence of early-onset CRC. This review synthesizes current advances in CRC epidemiology, risk factors, signaling biology, clinical presentation, screening, diagnosis, and management across the care continuum. We frame CRC as a systems-level disease in which genomic instability, epigenetic dysregulation, metabolic remodeling, tumor microenvironmental evolution, and gut microbiota interactions converge on interconnected pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, TGF-β, and immune-regulatory networks. We distinguish established standards of care from recent practice-changing developments and investigational strategies. Within this framework, we discuss blood-based screening, AI-assisted endoscopy, ctDNA-informed residual disease assessment, biomarker-defined molecular workup, immunotherapy strategies for dMMR disease, and targeted approaches for KRAS G12C-mutated, BRAF V600E-mutated, and HER2-positive metastatic CRC. Despite substantial progress, major challenges remain, including limited immunotherapy benefit in microsatellite-stable CRC, unequal access to high-quality screening and molecular testing, and uncertainty regarding implementation of newer biomarkers across diverse populations. An integrated framework linking population risk, tumor ecology, evidence-based biomarker use, and equitable precision care is essential for the next phase of CRC prevention and management.

title: Super-Resolution MRI-Derived Tumor-Stroma Ratio Phenotyping for Prognostic and Therapeutic Stratification in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound stromal heterogeneity that influences tumor progression, recurrence risk, and therapeutic response; however, stromal phenotypes are currently assessed by postoperative histopathology. Here, we developed a super-resolution MRI (srMRI)-based radiomics model to enable noninvasive tumor-stroma ratio (TSR) phenotyping in PDAC. Using multicenter cohorts comprising 737 patients, we constructed a srMRI-derived TSR-radscore capable of predicting pathological TSR with high accuracy (AUC = 0.870 and 0.791 in training and external validation cohorts). The TSR-radscore independently stratified recurrence-free survival and, when integrated with clinicopathological variables, improved early recurrence prediction in an independent surgical cohort. In a locally advanced PDAC cohort, srMRI-derived TSR was associated with distinct therapeutic outcomes, with H-TSR tumors showing improved survival under systemic therapy and an association with outcomes following immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination therapy. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that L-TSR tumors were enriched in extracellular matrix remodeling and TGF-β-related signaling pathways. Single-cell profiling further uncovered distinct cancer-associated fibroblast and T-cell states across TSR phenotypes, linking imaging-derived TSR patterns to underlying stromal and immune microenvironmental programs. Collectively, srMRI-derived TSR phenotyping provides a noninvasive and biologically interpretable biomarker for stromal characterization in PDAC, enabling improved recurrence-risk stratification and pre-treatment clinical assessment.

title: Transformer-Based Preoperative Invasiveness Identification and Postoperative Recurrence Risk Stratification in Stage T1N0M0 Lung Adenocarcinoma: A Multi-Center Cohort Study.
abstract: Surgery is the primary curative treatment for early-stage lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), with accurate identification of tumor invasiveness critical for determining pulmonary resection extent. Due to significant variability in postoperative recurrence among early-stage LUAD patients with aggressive tumors, a more effective risk stratification system is urgently needed to improve prognosis. This study developed the T1LUT system, a transformer-based tool for T1N0M0 LUAD management, covering preoperative tumor invasiveness identification and postoperative recurrence risk stratification. Preoperatively, a 3D Vision Transformer (ViT) with extra learnable tokens analyzes CT images. It outperforms 3D ViT with only CLS tokens, 2D ViT, and 3D ResNet across three independent test centers (Center D: 0.896 vs. 0.892, 0.879, 0.836; Center E: 0.906 vs. 0.837, 0.837, 0.835; Center F: 0.884 vs. 0.884, 0.881, 0.861), achieving higher mean AUROC to accurately assess invasiveness and guide surgical resection extent. Postoperatively, the multimodal IAC-PR model integrates CT images, reports, pathological data, and clinical/demographic information. It stratifies invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) patients into low-, medium-, or high-risk groups with an AUROC of 0.807 in testing-significantly better than single/partial-modal models. Validated via large-scale multicenter research, this system overcomes traditional assessment limitations, offering a robust tool for precise early LUAD treatment and improved prognosis.

It stratifies invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) patients into low-, medium-, or high-risk groups with an AUROC of 0.807 in testing-significantly better than single/partial-modal models. Validated via large-scale multicenter research, this system overcomes traditional assessment limitations, offering a robust tool for precise early LUAD treatment and improved prognosis.

title: Neuropathic Pain: From Mechanisms to Therapeutic Interventions.
abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by injury or disease of the somatosensory system. It involves peripheral nerve injury, central sensitization, transmitter imbalance, glial activation, and large-scale network remodeling. Despite substantial advances in pain biology, clinical assessment continues to rely predominantly on patient-reported symptoms, sensory examination, and conventional neurophysiological testing, approaches that often fail to delineate the predominant biological mechanisms underlying pain in individual patients. Recent advances in sensory phenotyping and multimodal imaging have enabled in vivo characterization of abnormalities at the receptor, neuroinflammatory, and circuit levels, thereby providing a foundation for mechanism-based stratification and more individualized therapeutic decision-making. This review summarizes neuropathic pain from clinical stratification to mechanism-based imaging and therapeutic intervention. We describe key clinical dimensions, including sensory gain, sensory loss, peripheral and central pain generators, mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain, central sensitization, and autonomic or small-fiber modifiers. These dimensions help explain why patients with the same diagnosis may show different symptoms and treatment responses. We also review major molecular mechanisms, including glutamatergic overactivity, GABAergic and glycinergic disinhibition, monoaminergic remodeling, and neuroimmune modulation. These changes reshape spinal, thalamocortical, limbic, salience, reward, cerebellar, and descending control circuits. Peripheral nerve ultrasound and MR neurography can help identify structural peripheral pain generators. PET, MRS, MRI, DTI, fMRI, EEG, and multimodal imaging can assess receptor availability, neurotransmitter balance, neuroinflammation, white matter integrity, and network connectivity. These imaging tools may link clinical phenotypes with biological mechanisms and help define mechanism-based subtypes. Imaging biomarkers may also support treatment selection, treatment monitoring, neuromodulation targeting, and translational trial design. This framework supports a shift from symptom-based assessment to mechanism-guided precision care for neuropathic pain.

title: Integrated Multi-Time-Point 18 F-FAPI PET/CT and Immune Histopathology for Predicting Pathological Complete Response in Microsatellite-Stable Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer Treated With Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy, Chemotherapy, and Immunotherapy.
abstract: Predicting pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy and chemotherapy remains challenging in microsatellite-stable (MSS) locally advanced rectal cancer. In this prospective exploratory study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06608537), 49 patients received short-course radiotherapy followed by sintilimab plus CAPOX and subsequently underwent radical surgery. We investigated whether treatment response could be better characterized by integrating two complementary biological dimensions: baseline immune organization and treatment-related stromal remodeling captured by multi-time-point 1 8 F-FAPI PET/CT. The pCR rate was 49.0% (24/49), and serial 1 8 F-FAPI imaging revealed distinct stromal kinetic patterns between response groups. Integration of intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structure (iTLS) count, B-cell density, preoperative tumor-to-iliacus muscle ratio (TIMR) at 30 min, and the delayed TIMR retention index from 90 to 120 min (RI 34 ) yielded a four-variable model with a mean AUC of 0.874 in repeated nested cross-validation. Complementary preclinical experiments provided functional support for a CAF-TGFβ-B-cell/TLS axis linking stromal regulation, immune organization, and treatment resistance. These findings highlight the complementary value of spatial immune organization and dynamic FAPI-defined stromal kinetics and provide a biologically informed framework for post-neoadjuvant, preoperative response stratification, pending prospective multicenter validation.

title: Intratumoral and Peritumoral Functional Connectivity Reveals Network-Level Signatures of Glioma.
abstract: Gliomas are recognized as network-level diseases that remodel functional connectivity across the brain. Using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from 306 patients with pathologically confirmed glioma at two hospitals, we delineated individualized intra- and peritumoral functional networks to quantify tumor-related alterations. Two novel indices-the ratio of intratumoral functional regions (RIFR) and ratio of peritumoral tumor-related regions (RPTR)-were proposed to describe network remodeling. Both indices were related to pathological, structural, functional, cognitive, language, and survival measures. Lower RIFR indicated diminished intratumoral connectivity and worse prognosis, while higher values reflected preserved network integration and longer survival. Models incorporating network features yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.90 in training and 0.86-0.88 in external validation. Supporting analyses suggested that intratumoral functional regions are associated with distinct molecular and cellular characteristics. These findings suggest that intra- and peritumoral networks reflect biologically and functionally distinct tumor subregions and are associated with network-level alterations, brain function, and patient outcome. Interpretation is limited by the hemodynamic basis of rs-fMRI, incomplete data, and limited intraoperative validation. These findings identify individualized intra- and peritumoral connectivity measures as candidate markers of glioma-associated network remodeling and prognosis that require prospective, multimodal validation.

title: Accuracy of Machine Learning in Differential Diagnosis of Multiple System Atrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is frequently misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease (PD) or progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), posing significant diagnostic challenges. Objective The aim of the study was to systematically evaluate the efficacy of machine learning (ML) in differentiating MSA from other neurodegenerative disorders. Methods We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (up to July 5, 2025), including ML-based MSA diagnostic studies. QUADAS-2 assessed bias risk, and a bivariate mixed-effects model synthesized diagnostic metrics. Results A total of 51 studies (comprising 3595 MSA patients and 18,189 total cases) were included in the systematic review. Of these, 38 studies contributed to the quantitative synthesis, whereas the remaining 13 studies were summarized qualitatively. In the primary analysis comparing MSA with PD, the pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.81-0.90), specificity 0.87 (95% CI: 0.83-0.90), and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve (AUC) 0.93 (95% CI: 0.90-0.95). Overall, pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (95% CI: 0.82-0.88), specificity 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89-0.94), and AUC 0.94 (95% CI: 0.92-0.96). Positron emission tomography (PET)-based models achieved optimal performance (sensitivity: 0.90, specificity: 0.96, AUC: 0.97), whereas deep learning models outperformed others (sensitivity: 0.93, specificity: 0.98, AUC: 0.99). Conclusion ML models integrating PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy for MSA. Future work should prioritize prospective multicenter validation and standardized external testing to facilitate clinical implementation.

title: Motor Cortex Disinhibition Is Dissociated from Clinical Motor Features in Parkinson's Disease: Longitudinal Evidence.
abstract: Background In Parkinson's disease, motor dysfunction largely reflects dopamine-dependent pathophysiological alterations and compensatory mechanisms that progress over time and are partially reversible with dopaminergic treatment. Our recent cross-sectional observations suggest that disinhibition of the primary motor cortex-assessed with short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) using transcranial magnetic stimulation-does not correlate with clinical motor features, does not progress across disease stages, and instead correlates with olfactory dysfunction, a common prodromal and dopamine-independent feature. Objective We aimed to provide longitudinal evidence for or against the hypothesis that motor cortex disinhibition is dissociated from clinical motor features in Parkinson's disease. Methods We compared SICI across three cohorts (total n = 95 patients): (1) baseline and 2-year follow-up (n = 43), with concurrent motor assessment and 18 F-DOPA positron emission tomography (PET) imaging (n = 24); (2) before and after levodopa administration (n = 30); and (3) before and after focused ultrasound subthalamotomy (n = 22). We also included a pooled healthy control group (n = 75) from two previously published studies. Bayesian statistics was applied to formally assess evidence for the presence or the absence of an effect. Results SICI was expectedly reduced, with very strong to extreme Bayesian evidence, in patients compared with control subjects. We found evidence that cortical disinhibition did not worsen with clinically evident disease progression confirmed with 18 F-DOPA PET and did not improve following a clinically effective dose of levodopa or subthalamotomy. Moreover, changes in SICI did not correlate with changes in motor features across cohorts. Conclusions These findings provide longitudinal evidence that motor cortex disinhibition is largely dissociated from clinical motor features in Parkinson's disease. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Preoperative Functional Imaging Predicts Deep Brain Stimulation Outcome in Craniocervical Dystonia.
abstract: Background Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established treatment for craniocervical dystonia (CCD), yet postoperative benefit varies widely and cannot be estimated before surgery. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has shown prognostic value across DBS indications. The objective of this study was to develop and externally validate preoperative rs-fMRI models estimating DBS response in CCD. Methods Forty-two patients from two independent centers underwent preoperative 3 T rs-fMRI (discovery, n = 26; validation, n = 16). Using 12 literature-informed, symptom-relevant regions of interest, we quantified the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation as a measure of intrinsic regional neural activity. We applied regularized modeling to classify super-responders, distinguish responders from non-responders, and estimate improvement in Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale motor subscore. Results When applied to the validation cohort, the imaging models achieved a three-category classification accuracy of 75.0% (50.5%-89.8%) using a sequential two-step procedure (P perm = 0.002). Predicted continuous improvement was also correlated with empirical improvement (R ext = 0.65, Q 2 = 0.34, P perm = 0.004). Within the discovery cohort, nested leave-one-out-cross-validation, in which feature selection and decision-threshold derivation were repeated independently within each training fold, yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.73 (0.50-0.96) and 0.77 (0.51-1.00). Across models, baseline primary motor cortex activity was consistently associated with diminished postoperative benefit. Conclusions Preoperative rs-fMRI captures clinically relevant variation in baseline brain state in CCD, with predictive performance supported in an external validation. These findings provide preliminary support for rs-fMRI as a potential source of information to aid patient counseling and clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Automated Magnetic Resonance Volumetry to Measure Multiple System Atrophy Disease Progression in Clinical Trials.
abstract: Background Recent studies have reported longitudinal brain atrophy in multiple system atrophy (MSA) in relatively small patient cohorts. Objective To compare longitudinal regional brain volume and clinical changes as endpoint measures for MSA clinical trials. Methods MSA patients with 1-year longitudinal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were selected from the placebo arm of the M-STAR Study (NCT03952806) and stratified into MSA-cerebellar (MSA-C) and MSA-parkinsonism (MSA-P) subtypes. A multisite healthy control (HC) cohort from international datasets was included for comparison. Baseline and longitudinal atrophy were assessed through automated MRI volumetry. Standardized longitudinal effect size values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and sample sizes required to detect treatment effect were estimated for 42 individual regional brain volumes, four combined volumetric indexes, nine clinical scales, and serum neurofilament light chain. Results The final study cohort included 129 MSA patients (76 MSA-C, 53 MSA-P) and 184 HC. The most atrophic structures at baseline were infratentorial regions in MSA-C and putamen in MSA-P. In both subtypes, infratentorial structures showed the largest longitudinal volume loss compared with HC. The annualized change of a cerebellum-pons-putamen volumetric index was the most powerful progression biomarker in MSA patients (effect size: -1.81 [95% CI: -2.14, -1.55]) and in both subtypes (MSA-C: -2.04 [95% CI: -2.58, -1.68], MSA-P: -1.55 [95% CI: -2.08, -1.22]), requiring the lowest sample size per arm (MSA, N = 55 to detect 30% treatment effect), and outperforming clinical measures (-59.6% patients required per arm). Conclusion These findings support longitudinal MRI-derived regional atrophy rates as sensitive imaging endpoints to assess treatment efficacy in MSA clinical trials. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Neuromelanin-Sensitive MRI as a Marker of Clinical Severity and Disease Burden in Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract: The neuropathology of Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized in part by the degeneration of catecholaminergic neurons, particularly dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC), yet no validated in vivo biomarker quantifies this process. Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (NM-MRI) enables noninvasive assessment of these neuronal populations, although relationships with clinical severity, disease burden, and progression remain incompletely defined. We conducted the first Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis examining associations between NM-MRI measures and clinical outcomes in PD, including subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses. Reduced NM-MRI measures were associated with greater motor impairment (18 studies; pooled r = -0.406), longer disease duration (14; r = -0.426), higher Hoehn and Yahr stage (10; r = -0.336), and higher levodopa equivalent daily dose (6; r = -0.337) (all P < 0.001). Thirty-nine studies (1983 patients with PD) were included in the systematic review. Narrative synthesis demonstrated distinct SNpc/LC associations: SNpc measures were primarily associated with motor dysfunction and disease stage, displaying hemispheric asymmetry, intranigral topography, and phenotype-specific patterns, whereas LC measures were preferentially linked to cognitive, affective, autonomic, and sleep-related symptoms. Four longitudinal studies (~1.5-3 years) reported declines in selected NM-MRI measures (~5%-19% annually). Multimodal studies suggested NM-MRI captures a complementary dimension of nigrostriatal pathology alongside dopaminergic, iron-sensitive, and diffusion-based markers. NM-MRI provides a biologically interpretable in vivo measure of catecholaminergic neuron integrity and survival in PD, with consistent cross-sectional associations with clinical disease burden. Emerging longitudinal and multimodal evidence supports its potential as a progression-sensitive imaging biomarker for disease-modifying clinical trials. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Identification of Variants in Two Families With Congenital Cataract by Whole Exome Sequencing.
abstract: Background Congenital cataract (CC) is an ophthalmic disorder diagnosed at birth or during early infancy, characterized by severe visual impairment and potential blindness. This study aimed to evaluate the pathogenicity of two variants: GJA8 c.201C>G (p.Asp67Glu) and CRYBB2 c.325A>T (p.Ile109Phe). Methods The patient's lenses were examined using slit-lamp photography and B-ultrasound. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and sanger sequencing were performed to identify the variants. Multiple sequence alignment was conducted using CLUSTALW to assess the evolutionary conservation of the affected residues. Structural modeling and conformational analyzes of wild-type (WT) and mutant-type (MT) proteins were conducted using AlphaFold2, PyMOL, and computational structural dynamics approaches, including root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) and normal mode analysis (NMA). Results Two likely pathogenic missense variants were identified in two unrelated families: c.201C>G (p.Asp67Glu) in exon 2 of GJA8, which encodes Connexin 50 (Cx50) protein, was paternally inherited in family 1, whereas c.325A>T (p.Ile109Phe) in exon 4 of CRYBB2 occurred de novo in family 2. The c.201C>G (p.Asp67Glu) variant mapped to the first extracellular loop (EL1) of Cx50. Structural modeling revealed disruption of the Asp67-Arg185 ionic interaction (Cα-OD distance: 3.4 → 4.9 Å) alongside a novel hydrogen bond with Asn63. Reduced RMSF in the mutant indicated localized rigidification of EL1, potentially impairing channel gating and correlating with severe cataract in affected family members. The co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype within the family 1 was confirmed by sanger sequencing combined with phenotypic analysis. The c.325A>T variant (p.Ile109Phe) in CRYBB2 increased protein flexibility, and the bulky aromatic phenylalanine side chain perturbed the hydrophobic core of Greek key motif III, causing global dynamic instability. The CRYBB2 c.325A>T variant was further confirmed to be de novo by sanger sequencing in conjunction with phenotypic analysis in family 2. Furthermore, multiple sequence alignment demonstrated that both residues are highly evolutionarily conserved. Conclusions This study expands the pathogenic spectrum of congenital cataract. Our findings provide novel insights into the molecular diagnosis of CC and have important implications for genetic counseling.

title: Free Innervated Gracilis Muscular Flap for Functional Abdominal Wall Reconstruction Following Desmoid Tumor Resection: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Desmoid tumors (DTs) are rare, benign, locally aggressive myofibroblastic neoplasms. Complete resection with negative margins remains the standard treatment despite their lack of metastatic potential. As DT commonly involve the anterior abdominal wall, their excision may result in complex defects requiring advanced reconstruction. We herein present the first functional single-stage reconstruction of an abdominal wall defect with the use of a free innervated gracilis muscle flap transfer. A 29-year-old woman, presented with a palpable tumor on the left-side of her abdominal wall. She underwent surgery and on biopsy, the tumor was diagnosed as a DT. The patient underwent wide resection through an abdominoplasty approach, which resulted in a rectus abdominis defect involving the anterior rectus abdominis sheath. The 8 × 7cm-sized defect was reconstructed with free transfer of a neurotized gracilis muscle flap, anastomosed to the deep inferior epigastric vessels, whereas, the anterior branch of the obturator nerve was coapted to the ninth intercostal nerve. Finally, a monofilament polypropylene mesh was used for reconstruction of the missing anterior rectus sheath. Ever since and during a follow-up of 5 years, electromyographic examinations have demonstrated excellent re-innervation of the gracilis muscle flap. The patient underwent regular follow-up examinations, including CT imaging at 1, 2, and 5 years postoperatively, with no evidence of abdominal wall protrusion or tumor recurrence. This case demonstrates that the free innervated gracilis flap can provide a safe and reliable reconstructive option for complex abdominal wall defects following oncologic resection.

title: Simultaneous T1, T2, R2*, PDFF, and triglyceride quantification in the head and neck using magnetic resonance fingerprinting on a 1.5T MR-Linac.
abstract: Background The extraction of quantitative biomarkers on the MR-Linac, which have been shown to be promising in the head and neck, remains a significant challenge due to the strict time constraints. Purpose The purpose of this study was to assess the technical feasibility of magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) to simultaneously extract quantitative T1, T2, R2*, PDFF, and triglyceride composition in the head and neck on the MR-Linac. Methods Inversion-prepared, multi-echo, golden angle radial, variable flip angle, MRF data were acquired on a 1.5T MR-Linac. The data were corrected for phase errors in the bipolar multi-echo acquisition followed by low rank reconstruction with total variation regularization. A dictionary of signals parameterized by T1/T2 was calculated with an extended phase graph algorithm. The singular images were constructed using a signal subspace from the dictionary and the first singular images were then jointly fit for R2* and PDFF using the off-resonance information from an independent B0 map. The complete set of B0/T2*-corrected fat-water separated water singular images were fitted for T1/T2. Triglyceride composition was computed using the multi-echo complex readout. Three phantoms and three healthy volunteers were assessed for accuracy, repeatability, and reproducibility against validated reference sequences across five days using a test-retest setup. Results All coefficients of determination were at least 0.9 against reference sequences in standard phantoms across all quantitative parameters. The repeatability and reproducibility averaged under 5% in phantoms and under 10% in healthy volunteers. Conclusion The proposed MRF acquisition demonstrated the potential to replace the current time-intensive sequences on the 1.5T MR-Linac, thus increasing the adoption of specialized quantitative imaging biomarker approaches at high temporal density in the head and neck.

title: Combined PET imaging of tumor hypoxia and proliferation in Glioblastoma using a single injection of 18F-FMISO and 18F-FLT: Association with sites of subsequent recurrence.
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intra-tumoral heterogeneity, rapid proliferation, hypoxia-driven radio-resistance, and early recurrence. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI, the standard of care imaging modality for surgical and radiotherapy planning, lacks specificity for viable tumor burden, particularly in non-enhancing regions. Purpose This pilot study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative dual-tracer PET using a combined dose of 18 FMISO (hypoxia) and 18 FLT (proliferation) improves tumor delineation and predicts subsequent local recurrence compared with MRI. Methods Seven patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas (5 GBM, 2 IDH-mutant astrocytomas) underwent preoperative dual-[FMISO+FLT] static PET at 180 min post-injection, and MRI. 6/7 patients underwent resection. Tumor volumes were segmented from PET, contrast-enhanced T1 (T1-Gd), and T2-FLAIR. Postoperative resection cavities were delineated, and follow-up MRI every 3 months was used to identify recurrence. PET-defined tumor volumes extending beyond resection were correlated with subsequent recurrence sites. Results Thirteen lesions were analyzed; all showed [FMISO+FLT] uptake (mean activity concentration ratio 1.6 with the cerebellar cortex used as reference region). PET-defined tumor volumes (9.2 cc) were slightly larger than T1-Gd (7.9 cc) but smaller than T2-FLAIR (28.8 cc). PET-defined volumes frequently extended beyond MRI-defined contours (mean non-overlap 6.4 cc vs T1-Gd; 1.5 cc vs. T2-FLAIR). Of six patients undergoing resection, four developed local recurrence within 3.3 months. In all cases, recurrence arose within PET-avid regions outside the resection cavity. The other two patients with complete resection of PET-defined volumes showed a relatively prolonged progression-free-survival (PFS) and including one patient with overall survival exceeding 36 months. Conclusions Dual-[FMISO+FLT] PET is feasible, safe, and can allow delineation of biologically viable tumor subregions, in particular within the MRI T2-FLAIR volume. This approach prospectively identified sites of subsequent local recurrence and may improve surgical planning and radiotherapy dose escalation. Larger validation studies are warranted to establish dual-tracer PET as a precision imaging paradigm in GBM.

title: Multimodal PET/MRI radiomics model for the classification of Alzheimer's disease and other dementia subtypes: A multicenter study.
abstract: Background Accurate and early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a major clinical challenge. This study aims to explore the value of multimodal positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics to improve diagnostic accuracy. Purpose To develop and evaluate hippocampus-based multimodal PET/MRI radiomics models for AD classification and exploratory five-class classification, and to compare early fusion (EF) with multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM)-based decision-level fusion. Method A total of 758 patients who underwent both PET ([18F]FDG and Amyloid-β) and MRI (3DT1, T1WI, T2WI, T2-FLAIR) were retrospectively included as the primary dataset in this study. 945 radiomic features (RFs) per sequence were extracted from the bilateral hippocampus. Models were evaluated on the primary cohort using a five-fold stratified cross-validation at the subject level (80% training and 20% testing in each fold). Feature selection was performed independently for each sequence using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). For multimodal PET/MR models, features from all six sequences were concatenated, and feature selection was applied (EF). Six classifiers were used to construct classification models for two tasks, including (1) AD/non-AD classification, and (2) exploratory five-class classification among AD, FTD, VaD, MCI, and other dementia. In addition, an MCDM-based strategy was implemented to fuse multimodal RFs and multi-classifiers. Modality-matched external validation was performed in an independent cohort of 45 patients with 3DT1 and Aβ PET available. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was employed to assess the clinical usefulness of the models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to explore the interpretability of the EF-based model. Results Among the 758 patients in the primary dataset, AD, FTD, VaD, and MCI were present in 481 (63.5%), 34 (4.5%), 15 (2.0%), 136 (17.9%) cases, with 92 (12.1%) classified as the other dementia subtypes. The MCDM-based models achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) for both tasks on the primary dataset (Task 1: AUC = 0.848; Task 2: AUC = 0.797), significantly higher than EF-based models in Task 2 (AUC = 0.782, p < 0.001) and showing comparable performance in Task 1 (AUC = 0.839, p = 0.629). On the external dataset, EF and MCDM models achieved AUCs of 0.741 and 0.761, respectively, for Task 1. The MCDM model showed a higher AUC than EF. DCA suggested potential net-benefit advantages for the multimodal models across selected threshold ranges. SHAP analysis identified wavelet-transformed texture features as the key predictors. Conclusion Hippocampus-based PET/MRI radiomics models showed promising performance for binary AD classification, with further improvement achieved by the MCDM strategy. The five-class findings should be regarded as exploratory. External validation provides preliminary support for the reduced 3DT1-Aβ PET model and does not establish the generalizability of the complete six-modality framework.

Accurate and early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a major clinical challenge. This study aims to explore the value of multimodal positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics to improve diagnostic accuracy.

To develop and evaluate hippocampus-based multimodal PET/MRI radiomics models for AD classification and exploratory five-class classification, and to compare early fusion (EF) with multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM)-based decision-level fusion.

Method

A total of 758 patients who underwent both PET ([18F]FDG and Amyloid-β) and MRI (3DT1, T1WI, T2WI, T2-FLAIR) were retrospectively included as the primary dataset in this study. 945 radiomic features (RFs) per sequence were extracted from the bilateral hippocampus. Models were evaluated on the primary cohort using a five-fold stratified cross-validation at the subject level (80% training and 20% testing in each fold). Feature selection was performed independently for each sequence using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). For multimodal PET/MR models, features from all six sequences were concatenated, and feature selection was applied (EF). Six classifiers were used to construct classification models for two tasks, including (1) AD/non-AD classification, and (2) exploratory five-class classification among AD, FTD, VaD, MCI, and other dementia. In addition, an MCDM-based strategy was implemented to fuse multimodal RFs and multi-classifiers. Modality-matched external validation was performed in an independent cohort of 45 patients with 3DT1 and Aβ PET available. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was employed to assess the clinical usefulness of the models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to explore the interpretability of the EF-based model.

Results

Among the 758 patients in the primary dataset, AD, FTD, VaD, and MCI were present in 481 (63.5%), 34 (4.5%), 15 (2.0%), 136 (17.9%) cases, with 92 (12.1%) classified as the other dementia subtypes. The MCDM-based models achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) for both tasks on the primary dataset (Task 1: AUC = 0.848; Task 2: AUC = 0.797), significantly higher than EF-based models in Task 2 (AUC = 0.782, p < 0.001) and showing comparable performance in Task 1 (AUC = 0.839, p = 0.629). On the external dataset, EF and MCDM models achieved AUCs of 0.741 and 0.761, respectively, for Task 1. The MCDM model showed a higher AUC than EF. DCA suggested potential net-benefit advantages for the multimodal models across selected threshold ranges. SHAP analysis identified wavelet-transformed texture features as the key predictors.

Conclusion

Hippocampus-based PET/MRI radiomics models showed promising performance for binary AD classification, with further improvement achieved by the MCDM strategy. The five-class findings should be regarded as exploratory. External validation provides preliminary support for the reduced 3DT1-Aβ PET model and does not establish the generalizability of the complete six-modality framework.

title: Deep learning-based CNN method for fiducial marker detection in kilovoltage X-ray images for liver tumor motion monitoring.
abstract: During radiation therapy, liver tumor motion can reduce dose delivery accuracy and increase irradiation of adjacent healthy tissues. Because liver tumors are difficult to visualize directly on kilovoltage (kV) X-ray images, fiducial markers are commonly implanted as surrogates for tumor position during treatment. Conventional marker-segmentation approaches such as template matching can lose accuracy when markers are obscured by bone, surgical clips, or stents. Although Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based approaches have shown strong performance for image analysis, their application has been constrained to more static organs such as the prostate or has used single-center and vendor-specific datasets, limiting assessment of model transportability across different institutions and anatomic sites. The aim of this study was to develop, integrate, and evaluate a CNN-based method for fiducial marker detection in kV X-ray images to support real-time image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) during liver radiotherapy using a multi-institutional, multi-platform dataset spanning both large and fast free-breathing motion and slow and small breath-hold motion. A compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was trained on 314,625 kilovoltage (kV) X-ray images encompassing 28 patients from the multi-institutional TROG 17.03 LARK clinical trial (NCT02984566). The model was validated using a hold-out set of 31,463 images (10%) from the same cohort of 12 patients and 55 treatment fractions, spanning three centers and three respiratory motion-management techniques. The CNN was tested on 4184 images from 16 patients and 55 fractions across three centers and three motion-management techniques. The ground truth for testing was manually segmented marker positions from every 10 degrees of gantry rotation for each fraction of each test patient. Based on AAPM guidelines (TG147 and TGB135.B), feasibility for clinical implementation was predefined as > 95% of marker positions being within 2 mm of the ground truth position in each dimension, and processing time less than 150 ms per image using a simulated real-time Kilovoltage Intrafraction Monitoring (KIM) framework. Additional evaluation metrics included sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC). For the unseen test patient data, the marker position was segmented by the CNN within 2 mm in 95.4% of frames on the X axis and 97.6% of frames on the Y axis, meeting AAPM criteria. Sensitivity reached 97.76%, specificity was 99.94%, and the AUC was 0.9964. No statistically significant difference in localization error was observed between breath-hold and free-breathing treatments, although this comparison was limited by the small number of free-breathing patients. Localization error differed significantly between Varian and Elekta linacs due to imbalance within the dataset. The processing time for each image was 50-60 ms using a NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 GPU. A CNN-based method for fiducial marker detection in the liver was developed and evaluated on multi-institutional kV X-ray images spanning free-breathing and breath-hold motion, as well as Varian and Elekta linac platforms. The method satisfied the predefined feasibility criteria for positional accuracy and computation time, supporting future translation toward clinical implementation.
