title: Quantitative and qualitative magnetic resonance imaging-based analysis to predict postoperative disease progression in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common abdominal malignancies and the third leading cause of cancer-related death globally. Predicting the postoperative prognosis of HCC remains an important area of clinical research. Many qualitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicators have been used for noninvasive and global assessment of HCC for diagnostic and prognostic purposes. However, the prognostic value of quantitative MRI parameters has not been extensively validated in multicenter cohorts. Objective This study aimed to verify whether MRI-based imaging features could improve prognostic prediction in patients with HCC. We developed prognostic models to predict the progression-free survival (PFS) of patients with HCC. Methods In this multicenter cohort study, 203 patients diagnosed with early- to intermediate-stage HCC were divided into a training dataset and an external validation dataset. In addition to clinical indicators, the candidates included qualitative and quantitative MRI data. Three noninvasive models were developed: the Clinical Model, the Radiological Model, and the Combined Model. The patients were stratified according to the risk of disease progression. Model performance was assessed through discrimination and calibration analyses, decision curve analysis was performed, and a clinical application was designed. In addition, the subgroups at different stages of the disease were analyzed, and PFS was compared between the high- and low-risk groups. Results Prognostic nutritional index, tumor-feeding vessels, mosaic architecture and the signal enhancement ratio (SER) parameter were identified as independent predictors of disease progression in patients with HCC. The Combined Model demonstrated superior performance compared with the Clinical and Radiological Models. The areas under the curve (AUCs) in the training dataset were 0.822, 0.748, and 0.795, whereas those in the validation dataset were 0.819, 0.758, and 0.677, respectively. The Combined Model also demonstrated favorable calibration and greater net clinical benefit on decision curve analysis. Its predictive ability remained consistent regardless of the Child-Pugh classification or Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stage. Conclusion This study highlights the important role of quantitative and qualitative MRI assessments in evaluating the prognosis of patients with HCC and emphasizes the predictive value of SER parameter. However, these findings should nevertheless be interpreted with caution given the relatively limited sample size, despite the use of bootstrap internal validation and external validation.

title: A two-stage framework for fast proton spot map generation in pencil beam scanning prostate SBRT planning.
abstract: Background In pencil beam scanning (PBS) proton therapy, treatment plans are encoded as proton spot maps (PSMs). Although deep-learning methods can rapidly predict three-dimensional (3D) dose distributions from patient anatomy and planning intent, there is still no widely adopted direct, non-iterative approach to convert doses into physically deliverable spot patterns. This limits end-to-end automation in treatment planning and adaptive replanning for PBS. Purpose We developed and retrospectively evaluated GenSpot, a two-stage framework that reconstructs a PBS PSM from CT and dose. This study focused on the dose-to-spots reconstruction step under controlled, achievable-dose conditions, using clinical Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions as input in a single-institution prostate stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) cohort. Methods GenSpot uses a physics-informed projected proton spot map (PrPSM) representation that projects individual proton spots through the CT using water-equivalent thickness and percentage depth dose (PDD) information, aligning the spots with the CT and dose voxel grid while preserving a linear relationship with spot weights. Our dataset comprised 1036 fields from 259 prostate SBRT plans, split into training, validation, and test sets in an 80%/10%/10% ratio. A 3D SwinUNETR model was trained to predict PrPSMs from CT and dose inputs. Field-specific PSMs were then reconstructed from the predicted PrPSMs using column-wise nonnegative Lasso regression with precomputed PDD curves. MC dose distributions from GenSpot and clinical PSMs were compared using voxel-wise mean absolute error (MAE), 3D gamma analysis (3%/3 mm, 10% low-dose threshold), and dose-volume histogram (DVH) metrics at the composite-plan level. Results Within the held-out test dataset, the selected SwinUNETR model achieved a mean PrPSM MAE of 0.06 ± 0.02 (normalized units) with high structural similarity to projected clinical PrPSMs. At the dose level, MC doses from GenSpot PSMs showed low MAE (0.07 ± 0.03 Gy in the nonzero-dose region) and high mean gamma passing rates (0.92 ± 0.05 at the field level and 0.99 ± 0.02 at the plan level). Composite-plan DVH metrics differences were generally within 1 Gy for targets and organs at risk, although the high-dose tail of the clinical target volume showed a modest systematic increase. Spot map complexity, measured by the number of energy layers and spot counts, was similar to that of clinical plans, with 20% more spots for GenSpot PSMs. For a four-field case, GenSpot PSM generation required approximately 2.9 ± 0.2 min excluding final MC recalculation. Conclusions GenSpot reconstructed machine-compatible PSMs from CT and clinical MC dose with close composite-plan dose agreement in a single-institution prostate SBRT cohort. These results support GenSpot as a rapid, physics-informed dose-to-spots reconstruction component under achievable-dose conditions. The present study does not establish performance for arbitrary predicted or adapted dose inputs, and final MC recalculation and standard QA remain required before clinical use. Further validation with non-idealized dose inputs, multi-institution data, higher-resolution dose representations, and dedicated optimization-based baselines is needed before broader clinical implementation.

title: Radiogenomic inference of transcription factor regulatory architecture associated with a high-risk CT phenotype in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether a CT radiomics-defined poor-prognosis phenotype in NSCLC is associated with reproducible transcriptomic programs and distinct transcription factor (TF) activity patterns. Methods This retrospective radiogenomic study used public datasets from The Cancer Imaging Archive. A prognostic radiomics model was developed from pretreatment CT in 402 patients from the NSCLC-Radiomics collection and evaluated in an independent cohort of 110 patients from the NSCLC Radiogenomics collection. Seven tumor-centered intra- and peritumoral regions were analyzed. Features were extracted from original, wavelet-, and Laplacian-of-Gaussian-filtered CT images. After preprocessing and training-cohort standardization, a LASSO-penalized Cox model was developed. The locked model retained eight features, all from the GTV+10-mm region, and was applied to the internal and external validation cohorts without refitting. The training-cohort median RadScore was used unchanged for Kaplan-Meier visualization. Matched transcriptomic data were analyzed using preranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA), target-gene-based TF activity inference, TF co-activity networks, exploratory regulator prioritization, unsupervised TF-state clustering, and LINCS-based perturbational analysis. Results The radiomics model achieved Harrell concordance indices of 0.785 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.767-0.793), 0.819 (95% CI, 0.788-0.833), and 0.785 (95% CI, 0.752-0.802) in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. The high-risk phenotype showed exploratory enrichment of proliferative and stress-adaptive programs, led by HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS (normalized enrichment score [NES] = 1.696, false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.045), with additional enrichment of MYC targets and inflammatory response. HALLMARK_HYPOXIA showed a positive directional trend but did not meet the prespecified exploratory threshold. GSVA provided complementary sample-level evidence for MYC targets, hypoxia, E2F targets, DNA repair, and cell-cycle activity. Eleven of 13 evaluated TFs met the prespecified FDR threshold, including YAP1, MYC, HIF1A, E2F3, STAT3, KLF4, E2F1, and TP53. Integrated analysis prioritized HIF1A, STAT3, TP53, YAP1, and E2F1/E2F3 as candidate regulatory nodes. Unsupervised clustering of all 110 radiogenomic patients, performed independently of radiomics risk labels, identified three exploratory TF-defined states: Hypoxia_Metabolic (n = 69), Cell_Cycle_E2F (n = 31), and Hippo_Mechanosensing (n = 10). LINCS-based analysis generated regulatory-state-associated compound hypotheses. Conclusions A CT radiomics-defined poor-prognosis phenotype in NSCLC is associated with coherent transcriptomic programs and an interpretable TF regulatory architecture. This framework links routine imaging phenotypes to latent tumor-control programs and supports regulatory-state-informed therapeutic hypothesis generation.

title: Artificial intelligence apps for medical image analysis using pyCERR and cancer genomics cloud.
abstract: Purpose To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out-of-the-box, AI-based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. Development and validation methods The framework comprises two main components: the Python-native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute-funded resource that supports cloud-hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute-hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open-source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user-friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI-based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose-volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal-tissue complication and tumor-control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr-radiological-radiotherapy-imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ-at-risk (OAR) and lung-nodule segmentation based on published models trained in-house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr-notebooks. Potential applications The framework facilitates end-to-end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

title: Low-dose CT denoising using a diffusion prior via score distillation sampling.
abstract: Background Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but amplifies noise, which can degrade diagnostic reliability. Recent studies have applied diffusion-based models to LDCT denoising and shown promising performance. However, many of these approaches require paired LDCT and normal-dose CT (NDCT) data or dose-specific retraining, and their reconstruction procedures are often strictly coupled to a predefined diffusion trajectory. Purpose This study proposes an optimization-based LDCT denoising framework that uses a pre-trained NDCT diffusion model as an image prior and can be applied across various dose levels without dose-specific retraining. Methods We formulate LDCT denoising as an optimization problem guided by a pre-trained score-based generative model (SGM) trained only on NDCT images. The Poisson data fidelity term enforces consistency with the measured projection data, whereas the score distillation sampling (SDS) term acts as a regularizer that guides the reconstruction toward the NDCT distribution learned by the pre-trained SGM. The denoised image is obtained by iteratively optimizing a projection-domain residual variable using the combined Poisson data fidelity gradient and SDS-based regularization gradient. Results The proposed method effectively suppressed noise while preserving fine anatomical structures across multiple dose levels using a single pre-trained diffusion model. Quantitative evaluations with respect to full-dose reference images and visual comparisons demonstrated competitive performance compared with supervised and self-supervised LDCT denoising baselines. Conclusions The results show that diffusion-based image priors can be leveraged across various low-dose levels within the proposed optimization-based denoising framework. Our work suggests that SDS-guided diffusion priors are a promising direction for LDCT denoising in data-limited settings.

title: Self-supervised multi-contrast MRI reconstruction via mask-guided frequency-domain fusion.
abstract: Background Multi-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MC-MRI) enables detailed tissue characterization by acquiring multiple contrast-weighted images from the same anatomical region. Redundancy across contrasts can improve reconstruction from under-sampled data. However, conventional deep learning approaches rely on fully-sampled, contrast-aligned datasets, which require long acquisition times. Extended scanning durations not only increase patient burden but may also introduce physiological risks, limiting the practical adoption of accelerated MC-MRI in clinical settings. Purpose This study introduces Self-MF, a self-supervised MC-MRI reconstruction framework that leverages contrast redundancy without requiring fully sampled target-contrast labels. The framework aims to provide a high-fidelity, scalable solution for reconstructing under-sampled multi-contrast images while preserving anatomical details and contrast fidelity. Methods Self-MF implements a contrast-aware self-supervised learning strategy that randomly partitions the acquired target k-space into input and held-out subsets, allowing the model to learn joint anatomical priors from under-sampled data without fully sampled target-contrast labels. A mask-guided frequency-domain conditioning module constructs reference-conditioned auxiliary frequency channels from auxiliary contrasts and acquired target measurements, enhancing the recovery of fine structural features during score-based reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on public datasets (IXI, fastMRI) and a clinical multi-coil dataset (SIAT), spanning multiple acceleration factors and undersampling patterns to assess robustness and generalizability. Results Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that Self-MF outperforms existing representative reconstruction methods across different contrasts, datasets, and acceleration factors. On the SIAT multi-contrast dataset, Self-MF achieved PSNR/SSIM values of 35.16/0.8870, 33.46/0.9054, and 35.31/0.9187 for T1WI, T2WI, and PDWI reconstruction under 2D random undersampling at R = 4, respectively. On the fastMRI brain dataset, Self-MF achieved 41.15 dB/0.9637 and 35.02 dB/0.8814 for T2WI reconstruction under R = 4 and R = 8, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared classical, learning-based, and diffusion-based baselines. Conclusions Self-MF provides an effective, self-supervised solution for high-fidelity MC-MRI reconstruction without fully sampled target-contrast labels. By combining contrast-aware self-supervision, frequency-domain conditioning, and diffusion-based reconstruction, the framework achieves superior image quality and robust anatomical preservation, representing a significant advancement for multi-contrast MRI in both research and clinical practice.

title: Convolutional neural network metal artifact reduction in ultra-high resolution photon counting detector CT of middle- and inner-ear implants.
abstract: Background Metallic inner- and middle-ear implants with submillimeter structures requiring ultra-high resolution (UHR) imaging invariably result in metal artifacts at CT, which can obscure adjacent microstructures and subtle pathologic findings. Current metal artifact reduction techniques can be less effective for small metal objects or metal in heterogeneous background anatomy, and can sometimes introduce new artifacts or noise. Purpose To develop and evaluate an image-domain convolutional neural network to reduce metal artifacts near inner- and middle-ear implants in UHR photon-counting-detector (PCD)-CT. Methods For network training, three stapes prosthesis models containing titanium and platinum were randomly oriented within a head-sized phantom and imaged on a PCD-CT with a UHR protocol. Metal and metal+artifact images were isolated by subtraction of the phantom background followed by CT number thresholding. Isolated artifact signal was enhanced via multiplication with a randomized factor ranging from one to a pre-determined artifact amplification scalar hyperparameter. Paired training inputs (with artifacts) and labels (without artifacts) were created by adding metal-free patient temporal bone images with metal+artifact and metal images, respectively. Combinations of 9 patient CT volumes and 24 metal CT volumes were used to create 216 CT volumes for training and validation with an 80%/20% training/validation split. The network was retrained with different amplification scalars (5, 10, 20, 30, 40) and with either mean-squared-error or mean-absolute-error loss functions to determine the optimal combination of these hyperparameters. The network was tested on 7 CT volumes from patients with three different implant types: stapes prostheses, cochlear implants, and a transverse sinus stent. Network performance was quantified through the artifact index, noise magnitude, CT number preservation of metal and bone, and dimensions of metal measured as the full-width at half-maximum of CT number line profiles. Results Networks trained with mean-squared-error demonstrated a trade-off between metal artifact reduction and preservation of bone CT number as the artifact amplification scalar changed. The trade-off was not observed when mean-absolute error was used. Using the network with hyperparameters that best preserved bone and reduced artifacts simultaneously (mean-absolute-error, amplification scalar 20), the artifact index was improved by 83.2% (p < 0.001) across all implant types, and image noise was reduced by 46.8% (p < 0.001). Artifact reduction was significantly better for cases with stapes prostheses than the other implant types (p < 0.004), although artifact index was still greatly improved for all implant types (91.1% for the stapes prostheses, 81.3% for the CI, and 72.9% for the transverse sinus stent). Metal implant dimensions were not significantly different between the network input and output images (p = 0.67). Conclusion An image-domain convolutional neural network with task-specific hyperparameters reduced artifact severity and image noise in UHR PCD-CT of different inner- and middle-ear implants without loss of fine image detail.

title: Low latency and generalizable dynamic MRI via L+S alternating gradient descent and minimization.
abstract: Background Dynamic MRI reconstruction often requires accurate, fast, and low-latency algorithms that generalize across multiple applications, sampling schemes, and rates, without problem-specific parameter tuning. Existing methods either lack generalizability or require extensive parameter adjustment. Purpose To develop generalizable, low-latency MRI reconstruction algorithms based on low-rank (LR) and low-rank + sparse (L+S) models that are accurate, fast, and require minimal parameter tuning across diverse dynamic MRI settings. Methods We propose a novel Alternating Gradient Descent and Minimization (AltGDmin) approach for L+S matrix recovery from column-wise undersampled measurements, and extend it to a 3-level hierarchical L+S model for dynamic MRI. A few-shot (FS) learning modification (AGM-L+S-FS) is introduced to enable near low-latency reconstruction with per-frame processing time comparable to or faster than scan time. A simpler LR-only variant is also evaluated. Results The proposed algorithms were validated on 6 prospective and 12 retrospective dynamic MRI datasets, covering cardiac, speech, and abdominal applications, with Cartesian, pseudo-radial, radial, and spiral sampling schemes. Experiments demonstrate accurate reconstruction, generalizability across datasets and sampling rates, and low-latency performance. Detailed comparisons with state-of-the-art LR, L+S, low-latency, and unsupervised deep learning methods show superior or comparable performance. Conclusions Our AGM-L+S-FS approach provide generalizable, fast, and low-latency MRI reconstruction across multiple dynamic MRI applications and sampling schemes, without the need for problem-specific parameter tuning.

title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI-accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real-time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. Acquisition and validation methods The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI-linear accelerator (MRI-linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open-source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Data format and usage notes The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient-specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030. Potential applications The DoseRAD2026 dataset enables benchmarking and development of fast dose calculation methods for radiotherapy applications. Potential use cases include rapid beam-level dose estimation for photon and proton therapy, MRI-based dose calculation in MRI-only and MRI-guided radiotherapy workflows, and support for real-time adaptive radiotherapy strategies.

title: Uncertainty-aware hybrid model for reliable navigation guidance in prostate biopsy.
abstract: Background Prostate biopsy - performed under ultrasound (US) guidance - is the only confirmatory procedure for diagnosing prostate cancer. If several systems aiming at improving the accuracy of tissue sampling for histopathological analysis exist, they often fail to adequately account for patient / tissue motion and deformation during the procedure or are not suitable for real-time guidance towards a pre-defined target. Purpose This work proposes a real-time assistance method to help urologists navigate between biopsy sites leveraging both 2D US and 3D US information. Methods The proposed hybrid framework combines three ResNet-18-based sub-networks with a Kalman filter to track the pose of the current 2D US frame within a reference 3D US volume acquired during the intervention. Two of the networks predict relative rigid transformations from pairs of US frames or frame/slice combinations extracted from the 3D volume. A third network predicts the registration error from a frame/slice pair and acts as a large-error detector. This error prediction module is integrated directly into the iterative registration process, to ensure robust tracking in the presence of tissue deformation or image artifacts, while also providing an uncertainty estimate of registration quality at each time step. The proposed framework was trained and evaluated on complex biopsy trajectories generated from a dataset of 847 3D US volumes acquired during real transrectal prostate biopsy procedures from 97 patients. The dataset was divided into training (78 patients, 669 volumes), validation (10 patients, 115 volumes), and test (9 patients, 63 volumes) sets. Performance was compared with an image-correlation-based baseline method using clinically relevant evaluation metrics, including the mean surface registration error (mean SRE) over 25-s trajectories, as well as the percentage of registered frames with an SRE below 2.5 mm and 5 mm. Statistical significance was assessed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (adjusted with Holm-Bonferroni correction) and 95% confidence bootstrap intervals (CI 95%) across the test cohort. Effect sizes were quantified with rank-biserial correlation (RBC). Results Compared with the baseline method, the proposed approach achieved a significant reduction in the mean SRE over 25-s trajectories, decreasing from 3.1[2.2,4.9] to 2.2[1.8,2.5] mm (median [CI 95%], p = 0.016, RBC = 0.96). In addition, the proposed large-error detector - used for uncertainty estimation - achieved a balanced accuracy score of 0.81 for classifying registration errors above or below a given threshold of 5 mm. Conclusions These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to improve the accuracy and robustness of real-time prostate biopsy navigation guidance.

title: Evaluation of quantitative accuracy in 4D DCE-bCT: Insights from a perfusion phantom study.
abstract: Background Four-dimensional dynamic contrast-enhanced breast CT (4D DCE-bCT) provides submillimeter spatial resolution and temporal sampling within seconds, offering potential for improved perfusion assessment in breast cancer. Its quantitative accuracy, however, must be validated. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of dynamic iodine concentration quantification in 4D DCE-bCT using a perfusion phantom with in-line optical spectroscopy and ultraviolet-visible (UV/VIS) spectrophotometry as reference standards. Methods A dynamic flow phantom with a 3 mm internal diameter was used to approximate tumor-feeding vessels. Potassium iodide (KI) contrast was introduced using block-pulse injections at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL and a gradual inflow-outflow protocol to reproduce bolus passage. In-line optical spectroscopy and UV/VIS spectrophotometry provided reference measurements. Dynamic bCT acquisitions were performed using a previously developed sparse-view protocol. A static pre-contrast scan was reconstructed with the iterative maximum-likelihood polychromatic algorithm for CT (IMPACT), and post-contrast dynamic scans were reconstructed using the prior image constrained compressed sensing (PICCS) algorithm. Acquisitions were performed at 65 kV with 0.25 mm Cu filtration, 80 mA for the pre-contrast scan (300 projections over 10 s) and 32 mA for the post-contrast scans (444 projections per 100 s), using a 5 ms pulse width. Projection data were corrected for scatter and motion before reconstruction, and the static prior was then subtracted from post-contrast volumes. Object-size effects were evaluated using the 3 mm tube and 5, 10, 15, and 20 mm hollow spheres filled with non-flowing iodine at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL. The tube interior was segmented using thresholding and morphological cleanup, while spherical phantoms were segmented by identifying the sphere center and extracting all enclosed voxels. Voxel values were converted to iodine concentration using a pre-determined calibration curve, and agreement with reference standards was evaluated using peak concentrations and time-concentration profiles, with errors reported as absolute and relative differences. Results In dynamic block-pulse experiments, peak iodine concentrations measured by 4D DCE-bCT were systematically underestimated relative to ground truth, with relative errors of approximately 12% to 39%. In gradual inflow-outflow experiments, the peak iodine concentration derived from 4D DCE-bCT was 5.24 ± 0.61 mg I/mL, whereas optical ground truth measured 5.17 mg I/mL. Static experiments demonstrated an average underestimation of 0.23 ± 0.14 mg I/mL across target sizes and concentrations and no relationship between iodine estimation and target size. Conclusion 4D DCE-bCT enabled acquisition of time-varying iodine concentration profiles in a 3 mm tube phantom. Gradual changes were captured more accurately compared to rapid changes, consistent with temporal averaging. These results demonstrate the feasibility of dynamic iodine imaging with 4D DCE-bCT while highlighting current limitations and motivating further evaluation in anatomically realistic phantoms and pilot clinical studies.

title: A dual-prompt framework combining spatial-mask priors and clinical-text conditioning for CT-only GTV delineation in esophageal cancer: A multicenter study.
abstract: Background Accurate gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation is essential for esophageal cancer radiotherapy, but CT-only automatic delineation remains difficult because of indistinct tumor boundaries. Purpose This study aimed to develop and validate a two-stage dual-prompt framework combining a spatial-mask prior with LLaMA3-encoded clinical-text conditioning for primary esophageal GTV delineation. Methods This multicenter study included 857 patients: 500 for development, 125 for internal validation, 50 for ablation analysis, and 182 for external validation. The proposed framework consists of two stages: (1) a CT-based automatic segmentation network generating an initial GTV as a spatial mask prompt, and (2) a refinement network that jointly incorporates spatial mask prompt and LLaMA3-encoded clinical text prompt derived from structured clinical information. Performance was evaluated using overlap, surface distance, and volumetric metrics, and compared with multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models. Ablation and radiomics analyses assessed component contributions and downstream consistency. Results In internal validation, the framework achieved a DSC of 80.32 ± 6.65%, an HD95 of 11.42 ± 8.90 mm, and an absolute volume difference of 9.99 ± 10.49 mL; all Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001 versus the comparison models. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the external cohorts. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the two external cohorts, respectively. In external cohort A, ContextUNETR showed a lower mean HD95 than the proposed model (10.93 ± 8.03 vs. 13.44 ± 18.90 mm), although the paired difference was not statistically significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.906). Compared with the direct Stage-1 output, the complete framework consistently improved overlap, boundary-distance, and volumetric-agreement metrics across the internal and both external validation cohorts (all adjusted p < 0.001). LLaMA3 encoding improved DSC versus an MLP using the same variables (adjusted p = 0.009), whereas ASSD did not differ significantly. Automatic and manual GTVs showed high radiomic concordance and comparable prognostic performance. Conclusion The framework improved overlap and volumetric agreement for CT-only primary esophageal GTV delineation across multicenter validation cohorts, although boundary-distance performance varied across external cohorts.

title: Joint segmentation and landmark detection for cardiac MRI with multi-scale inter-task feature fusion and gradient-bridged anatomical constraints.
abstract: Background Segmentation and landmark detection are essential yet complex tasks in Cardiac MRI (CMR) for quantitative assessment of the heart. Existing automatic CMR analysis methods typically handle the two tasks independently, overlooking their synergies that could improve the performance of both tasks. Purpose To develop an accurate and efficient multi-task learning (MTL) framework that jointly performs segmentation and landmark detection for CMR. Methods The proposed SLaDNet-GaB framework integrates a Segmentation and Landmark Detection Network (SLaDNet) with a Gradient-as-Bridge (GaB) loss. SLaDNet adopts a shared feature encoder and two separate decoders to generate segmentation and landmark predictions, respectively. Inter-Task Feature Fusion (ITFF) modules are inserted between the decoders at multiple resolution scales to facilitate bidirectional information exchange via channel-wise attention. Along with two intra-task losses, the dedicated GaB loss is further introduced during training to enforce inter-task anatomical consistency. Specifically, the loss guides the predicted landmarks toward the segmentation objective boundaries using gradient maps. We comprehensively evaluated the proposed method against both single- and MTL baselines on two public CMR datasets: a cine dataset (ACDC; 105/15/30 subjects for training/validation/testing) and a T1 mapping dataset (STONE; 150/20/40 subjects for training/validation/testing). Results SLaDNet-Gab outperformed the baselines in both segmentation (dice scores: 92.37/94.27% on ACDC/STONE, p < 0.05) and landmark detection (point-to-point distances: 2.22/1.51 voxels on ACDC/STONE, p < 0.05). For downstream tasks, the proposed method consistently achieved lower strain and T1 quantification errors than the other methods in most myocardial segments, with per-segment measurements closely agreeing with the manually derived values. Moreover, SLaDNet-GaB demonstrated relatively low training times (11.4/3.2 hours on ACDC/STONE) and an inference time of 6.12 msec./sample suitable for clinical adoption. Conclusions The proposed multi-tasking method achieves improved accuracy in CMR segmentation, landmark detection, and downstream quantification, while maintaining high computational efficiency.

title: Dosimetric impact of intrafractional ocular motion in LINAC-based ocular SRS/SRT: Defining real-time eye-tracking thresholds.
abstract: Background Photon-based LINAC ocular stereotactic radiosurgery and stereotactic radiotherapy (SRS/SRT) offer a noninvasive treatment approach for ocular malignancies. However, intrafractional ocular motion can compromise target coverage because of steep dose gradients and small treatment margins. Although ocular position monitoring and motion-management techniques have been investigated previously, quantitative dosimetric guidance relating angular gaze deviation to target and OAR degradation in modern LINAC ocular SRS/SRT remains limited. Purpose To characterize the dosimetric effects of simulated gaze deviation in photon-based LINAC ocular SRS/SRT, identify planning and geometric factors associated with motion robustness, and derive dosimetrically informed gaze-deviation thresholds for real-time eye tracking. Materials and methods Ninety-eight previously generated photon-based ocular SRS/SRT plans were retrospectively analyzed for ocular motion robustness using an Eclipse scripting approach. Planning target volumes (PTVs) were derived from hybrid CT-MRI and synthetic datasets based on clinically treated plaque brachytherapy cases, with a median PTV of 2.37 cc in the primary cohort. An ocular motion model was developed to simulate gaze deviations from 0° to 30° across 36 sampled directions per deviation level while incorporating both rotational and translational globe motion. All plans were prescribed 25 Gy in one fraction. A total of 109, 368 simulated dose evaluations were analyzed in the primary D95-normalized cohort, with corresponding PTV D98-normalized plans used to evaluate the effect of prescription normalization. Additional paired subgroup analyses evaluated beam energy (6 MV FFF vs. 10 MV FFF), MLC configuration (standard MLC vs micro-MLC), and PTV margin size (2 vs. 1 mm). The primary robustness endpoint was maximum safe gaze deviation, defined using preservation of simulated V100 ≥ 90%. Additional analyses evaluated OAR doses and associations between baseline geometric and dosimetric variables and motion robustness. Results Target coverage progressively deteriorated with increasing simulated gaze deviation. Using V100 ≥ 90% as the prespecified target-coverage criterion, at least 75% of D95- and D98-normalized plans maintained acceptable worst-direction coverage through approximately 6° and 9°, respectively. Optic nerve D0.03 cm 3 increased with gaze deviation, with the 75th percentile remaining at or below 12.1 Gy through approximately 7° for D95-normalized plans and 6° for D98-normalized plans. Lens D0.03 cm 3 exceeded the 5-Gy reference threshold in most plans at baseline and was therefore not used to determine a motion threshold. Greater target distance from the globe center strongly predicted reduced motion robustness, whereas larger target volume was associated with greater robustness. Higher plan conformity was also associated with increased motion sensitivity. Beam energy, MLC configuration, PTV margin, and tumor directionality had less practical influence on the derived robustness thresholds. Conclusions Photon-based LINAC ocular SRS/SRT demonstrated progressive target-coverage loss and increasing selected OAR doses with increasing simulated gaze deviation. Considering both target coverage and optic nerve dose, an approximately 5° gaze deviation represents a reasonable dosimetrically informed starting point for prospective real-time ocular motion monitoring. Because robustness varied substantially among plans, this value should not be considered a universal clinical threshold, and plan-specific assessment may ultimately support more accurate individualized gaze tolerances.

title: Impact of dose reduction and multi-parametric harmonization on multi-organ radiomics robustness in total-body PET imaging: Methodological implications for quantitative theranostics.
abstract: Background Radiomic features derived from positron emission tomography (PET) are sensitive to count statistics and acquisition protocol variability, thereby limiting quantitative reliability in low-dose and multi-center total-body PET imaging. Purpose This study evaluated dose robustness of PET radiomics and assessed the impact of multi-parameter ComBat harmonization on feature reproducibility. Methods A multi-center total-body PET dataset comprising 550 patients from two institutions was retrospectively analyzed. Seven dose levels were simulated from list-mode data (Standard; dose reduction factors (DRF) of 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, and 100). Automatic deep learning-based segmentation was applied. A total of 107 Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomic features were extracted from standardized uptake value (SUV)-normalized images. Feature-level ComBat harmonization was performed under five configurations (scanner manufacturer, pixel spacing, radiopharmaceutical, scatter correction, and non-harmonized baseline). Reproducibility was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC (2,1)) across dose levels, organs, and harmonization settings. Results Dose reduction produced organ- and feature-dependent effects. Overall, 32.7% of the features achieved good or excellent reproducibility (ICC ≥ 0.75) in at least one anatomical region. Selected first-order and intensity-associated features retained good reproducibility in several anatomical regions under moderate dose reduction (DRF ≤ 20), whereas severe count reduction (DRF 50-100) was associated with greater organ- and feature-dependent instability, particularly among higher-order texture features in vascular and lower-contrast soft-tissue regions. Harmonization produced organ and feature-dependent changes but did not uniformly improve cross-dose reproducibility or compensate for noise-induced instability. Conclusion Radiomics robustness in total-body PET is strongly influenced by dose level, anatomy, and acquisition variability. Moderate dose reduction preserves selected intensity-based features, while extreme count reduction compromises higher-order textures. Harmonization altered reproducibility patterns but did not uniformly improve cross-dose agreement or fully offset noise-induced instability, underscoring the need for dose-aware feature selection in multi-center PET radiomics.

title: A simple and interpretable method to predict head and neck offline adaptation needs based on anatomical changes.
abstract: Background Modern radiotherapy techniques do not automatically account for anatomical changes during treatment, which can lead to reduced target coverage, hotspots, or increased dose to healthy tissues. Adaptive Radiotherapy (ART) addresses this by updating the treatment plan based on the patient's current anatomy. In routine clinical practice, the decision to replan is often triggered by a suboptimal fit of the immobilization mask, identified by the radiation therapy technologist. Because this process is operator dependent and lacks methodological rigor, a quantitative decision-support method could substantially improve the replanning decision. Daily image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) images provide valuable clinical information but often lack sufficient quality for accurate target contouring or reliable dose calculation to support straightforward clinical decision-making. This limitation motivates the need for a simpler, more practical, and scalable alternative. Purpose This study develops an automated workflow to predict the need for replanning at every treatment fraction in head and neck (H&N) cancer patients using robust tools, thus requiring minimal manual validation while aiding the radio-oncologists in their decision-making. Methods A retrospective dataset of 21 H&N cancer patients treated on a Tomotherapy Radixact system (Accuray, USA) with kVCT daily imaging was analyzed, of whom 14 underwent replanning during treatment. For each patient, the planning CT (pCT) and daily images were processed in RayStation treatment planning system (RaySearch Laboratories AB, Sweden) via scripts. Rigid registrations were used to align daily images to the pCT, and a patient-specific region of interest (ROI) was defined to consistently capture the same anatomical region across all treatment fractions. ROI volumes were intersected with the external contour and converted to relative volumetric changes with respect to the pCT. By grouping patients according to whether a replanning occurred during treatment, differences in mean volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients were assessed at each treatment fraction. To automatically detect clinically relevant anatomical changes, a simple, interpretable model based on three volumetric features (current volume loss, short-term trend, and long-term trend) was evaluated using cross-validation. Thresholds defining the trigger condition were optimized using a tailored loss function that prioritizes early detection and penalizes false negatives more strongly than false positives. Model variants using different feature subsets and hyperparameters were compared, and the final configuration was selected prioritizing recall, followed by specificity and early flagging. Results Significant differences in volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients emerged at fraction 6 and remained significant for most subsequent fractions. The smallest adjusted p -values occurred around fractions 22-25. Using leave-one-out cross-validation, the best-performing model flagged patients to be replanned with 93% recall, doing so on average 8.4 fractions before clinical intervention. Conclusions Consistent differences in local tissue volume loss between replanned and non-replanned patients enabled the development of a simple automated workflow that triggers replanning for offline ART when learned volumetric thresholds are exceeded. This approach provides an objective complement to physician judgement and integrates seamlessly into existing IGRT workflows.

Significant differences in volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients emerged at fraction 6 and remained significant for most subsequent fractions. The smallest adjusted p -values occurred around fractions 22-25. Using leave-one-out cross-validation, the best-performing model flagged patients to be replanned with 93% recall, doing so on average 8.4 fractions before clinical intervention.

Conclusions

Consistent differences in local tissue volume loss between replanned and non-replanned patients enabled the development of a simple automated workflow that triggers replanning for offline ART when learned volumetric thresholds are exceeded. This approach provides an objective complement to physician judgement and integrates seamlessly into existing IGRT workflows.

title: Segment anything model (SAM)-driven prompt-guided interactive delineation of gross tumor volume for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Segment Anything Model (SAM), a prompt-guided foundation model, exhibits substantial potential for medical image segmentation by incorporating prior knowledge through user-defined prompts. However, the application of SAM in radiotherapy target delineation remains limited. Purpose This study proposes a feasible prompt-guided interactive delineation workflow driven by an optimized SAM. Methods A total of 100 rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy cases were collected (60 for training and 40 for testing). This study utilized bounding-box prompts to guide SAM for GTV segmentation. Physicians manually draw box prompts on certain slices, while box prompts for the remaining slices are automatically generated using an interpolation strategy. Four fine-tuning strategies for SAM training were evaluated, and the impact of prompt numbers and placements was assessed as well. The performance of the finalized workflow with optimized SAM was compared with five state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, and its robustness to prompt variations in middle-slice selection and box-prompt margins was analyzed. Results Compared to other fine-tuning methods, freezing the image encoder obtained the most stable performance. Prompts on only 3 slices achieved accuracy comparable to prompts on all slices. The placement of the middle-slice prompt exhibited negligible impact (p > 0.05). The finalized SAM-driven workflow outperformed end-to-end baseline models both visually and quantitatively (3D DSC: 0.92 vs 0.80; 3D HD95: 2.73 vs 12.70; IoU: 0.86 vs 0.67; Sensitivity: 91.20% vs 85.98%; Precision: 93.65% vs 79.23%), while maintaining stable performance across certain prompt variations. Conclusions The proposed SAM-driven interactive workflow with as few as 3 box prompts achieves favorable accuracy of GTV segmentation for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

title: Model-based image restoration targeting higher-dose digital mammography: Impact on radiologists' detection of clustered microcalcifications.
abstract: Background Image noise in digital mammography (DM) can obscure image details and reduce the detectability of clinically relevant findings such as microcalcifications. Purpose To present and evaluate an extended model-based (MB) image restoration pipeline for DM that incorporates quantum, electronic, and structural noise components, as well as spatial noise correlation, and to assess its effect on breast radiologists' detection of simulated microcalcification clusters in clinical mammograms. Methods A total of 120 clinical DM images acquired using a GE Senographe Pristina system were used. Simulated microcalcification clusters were inserted into locally dense fibroglandular regions at controlled contrast levels. The restoration pipeline was configured to target the signal and noise characteristics predicted by the model for an acquisition at approximately twice the original radiation dose. Six breast radiologists with different levels of experience, classified as Junior or Senior, participated in two human observer experiments: (i) a pilot study using original clinical images with simulated clusters and a four-alternative forced-choice (4AFC) protocol combined with a three-down-one-up (3D1U) staircase to estimate reader-specific contrast detection thresholds and achieve comparable baseline task difficulty across readers; and (ii) a main 4AFC observer study using individualized datasets generated according to each reader's estimated contrast threshold, in which microcalcification detection performance was compared between the original and restored image conditions based on the percentage of correct responses (PC). Two generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were used: the first evaluated the effect of image condition as a fixed effect, with reader and case as crossed random intercepts, and the second evaluated the effect of reader experience on detection performance in the original image condition. Results At the reader-specific contrast thresholds estimated in the pilot study, the mean PC for the original images was 78.3%, within the prespecified target performance range. Mean PC increased to 84.3% for the restored images, corresponding to an absolute improvement of 6.0 percentage points. The primary GLMM indicated a significant restoration effect on detection performance (OR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.15-2.14, p=0.005 ). Baseline mean PC was 78.7% for Junior readers and 78.0% for Senior readers, and the separate GLMM found no evidence of an experience-group effect under the original image condition ( p=0.858 ). Conclusions The proposed extended MB restoration pipeline improved the detectability of simulated microcalcification clusters by breast radiologists under the controlled 4AFC conditions investigated. By targeting the signal and noise characteristics predicted by the model for an acquisition at approximately twice the original radiation dose without requiring additional radiation exposure, the method represents a promising approach for improving microcalcification detectability in DM.

title: A generalizable 3D dose prediction across heterogeneous cohorts: A framework developed for the 2025 AAPM GDP-HMM challenge.
abstract: Background Manual radiotherapy treatment planning is labor-intensive, subjective, and highly variable across planners and institutions. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach for estimating achievable three-dimensional (3D) dose distributions for a given plan (hereafter: dose prediction) by directly mapping patient anatomy and beam geometry to voxel-wise dose. However, achieving robust generalization across diverse anatomical sites, prescriptions, and institutions remains a major challenge, particularly under computational constraints required for clinical deployment. Purpose We sought to develop and evaluate a generalizable, computationally efficient 3D dose prediction framework capable of spanning heterogeneous multi-site and multi-cohort datasets, as defined in the 2025 AAPM Generalizable Dose Prediction for Heterogeneous Multi-Cohort and Multi-Site (GDP-HMM) Grand Challenge. Our goal was to design a model that not only achieved state-of-the-art voxel-wise accuracy but also maintained clinically meaningful dose-volume and geometric characteristics across diverse cases. Methods We implemented a fully convolutional 3D dose-prediction model adapted from the MedNeXt architecture, which was originally introduced as a high-capacity convolutional backbone for medical image segmentation and is well suited to volumetric dense prediction tasks. The network accepted multimodal inputs comprising CT, PTV/OAR masks, beam and angle plates, and scalar plan metadata. A composite loss function combined voxel-wise L 1 , body-masked weighted L 1 , structure-wise moment-matching, and gradient-based penalties to jointly preserve spatial fidelity and dosimetric accuracy. The model was trained on the fixed GDP-HMM dataset consisting of 2876 training plans, 356 validation plans, and a held-out test set of 498 plans using random 3D patches and evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE), homogeneity index (HI), and conformity indices (CI100%, CI50%). Ablation studies quantified the contribution of each loss component to overall performance. Statistical comparisons used paired Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction. Results The proposed model achieved a mean voxel-wise MAE of 2.04 Gy on the validation set, outperforming the challenge baseline (2.54 Gy). An ensemble with the baseline further improved MAE to 1.94 Gy on the validation set and 2.071 Gy on the held-out test set, corresponding to the lowest test-set MAE and first-place overall ranking in the GDP-HMM Challenge. Predicted dose distributions preserved key plan characteristics, with ΔHI, ΔCI 100% , and ΔCI 50% narrowly centered around zero, indicating consistent target coverage and dose conformity. Protocol-specific evaluations for head-and-neck and lung cohorts demonstrated close alignment with reference plans, with no systematic degradation in OAR endpoints. Ablation experiments showed that removing gradient-based terms increased MAE by 0.50 Gy, while excluding the moment-matching term increased MAE by 0.06 Gy confirming that both gradient- and moment-based constraints enhanced spatial and dosimetric fidelity. Conclusion We present a generalizable 3D dose prediction framework that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while satisfying stringent runtime requirements (< 3s per case on < 24 GB GPU memory). By integrating gradient-aware and moment-based constraints within a MedNeXt backbone, the model preserved clinical DVH endpoints and geometric plan features. These findings demonstrate that carefully engineered loss formulations are pivotal for cross-institutional generalization. The framework offers a foundation for rapid dose prediction that could accelerate treatment planning, reduce inter-planner variability, and enable intelligent automation in radiotherapy workflows.

title: Bilateral Breast Gradient Insert Prototype for Strong Diffusion Encoding at 3 T.
abstract: Purpose Diffusion MRI has shown promise for breast cancer screening, lesion characterization, and treatment response monitoring without contrast agents, but further translation is constrained by the gradient performance of conventional systems. The aim of this work is to develop a single-axis high-performance bilateral plug-and-play breast gradient insert to enable strong-gradient diffusion MRI. Methods An in-house breast gradient insert and bed-tabletop was constructed entirely from commercially available materials, providing a cost-effective solution compatible with existing MRI systems. Its wiring pattern was optimized for torque and force balancing, power dissipation, and target field performance. Evaluation included gradient field characterization, peripheral nerve stimulation simulation verification, and temperature and eddy current assessment. The setup was used for imaging of a diffusion phantom based on soy lecithin across a range of b values. Results Gradient efficiency ranged from 0.61 to 2.8 mT/m/A, enabling diffusion MRI using local strengths up to 420 mT/m (150 A). No peripheral nerve stimulation was observed during tests on five healthy volunteers. Eddy currents were successfully characterized, revealing a linear first order component with an amplitude of 0.03% of the applied gradient field. Imaging experiments demonstrated the feasibility of acquiring b = 10 000 s/mm 2 volumes with a TE of 78 ms, compared with 161 ms when using the scanner gradients (40 mT/m). Conclusion This work demonstrates a dedicated bilateral breast gradient insert for safe and feasible strong-gradient breast diffusion MRI and represents a first step toward dedicated hardware for breast cancer detection and characterization without contrast agents.

title: Independent Component Analysis for Non-Contrast-Enhanced Free-Breathing Pulmonary Ventilation and Perfusion MRI.
abstract: Purpose To introduce a robust approach for non-contrast-enhanced free-breathing functional lung MRI based on independent component analysis (ICA), addressing key limitations of standard methods such as sensitivity to irregular breathing or irregular heartbeat. Methods Repeated dynamic single-slice MRI of ten healthy volunteers and twenty-five lung tumor patients was performed in free breathing on a 0.35T MR-linac using a 2D coronal cine bSSFP sequence, resulting in 143 datasets. Following motion correction, lung segmentation, and signal alignment, temporal ICA was applied to extract ventilation and perfusion components. Ventilation- and perfusion-weighted maps were generated and compared to Fourier decomposition (FD) and matrix pencil (MP) analysis. Signal construction performance was evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient and nonparametric statistical testing, comparing the methods under regular and irregular breathing and heartbeat conditions. Map accuracy and robustness at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) were additionally assessed in numerical-phantom simulations. Results In vivo, ICA effectively separated physiological lung signals, achieving significantly higher temporal agreement with original voxel time courses than both FD and MP (all p<0.001 ). Under all physiological conditions, ICA yielded the highest temporal correlations. In simulations, ICA maintained robust signal fidelity, especially under irregular breathing and low-SNR conditions, preserving >90% of contrast in simulations, while FD and MP exhibited pronounced degradation and significantly reduced temporal correlations. Conclusion ICA functional lung MRI provides a robust alternative to conventional techniques, enabling reliable ventilation and perfusion assessment from free-breathing acquisitions, particularly in the presence of irregular respiratory patterns and motion.

title: Inertial Navigation Assisted Motion Correction for Brain MRI.
abstract: Purpose To assess the utility of inertial sensors for estimating parameters describing rigid body motion of the head, and to reduce motion related artifact through a hybrid prospective steering of the rotation via the sensor and retrospective realignment of translation via the MRI data. Theory and methods Inertial sensors are widely used for Earth navigation problems. However, drift accumulation from integrating noisy signals makes them impractical for MRI motion correction at millimeter resolution over minute-long scans. Prior work has shown that the MRI system's B0 and gravity are approximately orthogonal and can be exploited as reference vectors for 3-DOF orientation estimation. We introduce a hybrid inertial measurement-based method, which uses these fields to estimate 3-DOF orientation directly, without integration, thereby eliminating random walk. The remaining 3-DOF translation is recovered via phase correlation from the MRI data. We validate the efficacy of this hybrid method retrospectively using a 3D radial koosh-ball sequence and prospectively using 2D EPI time-series acquisition during volunteer motions. Results IMU-based orientation estimation followed by phase correlation achieved a mean accuracy of 0.6° and 0.4 pixels across all experiments. Image quality improved when motion correction was applied in all volunteer scans for both retrospective and prospective correction cases. Conclusion The proposed method measured head motion in the MRI scanner with high accuracy at unprecedented sampling rates and enabled both retrospective and prospective correction, improving image quality by aligning k-space data and reducing motion artifacts.

title: NR-MRC: A No-Reference Magnetic Resonance Curve Estimation Network for Tumor MR Image Quality Assessment and Enhancement.
abstract: Purpose Accurate image quality assessment (IQA) is essential for evaluating tumor magnetic resonance (MR) images in clinical practice and computer-aided diagnosis. However, most existing IQA models are designed for natural images and require reference images for training. Variability in tissue characteristics, lesion location, and lesion morphology, together with the scarcity of high-quality MR reference images, makes quality assessment of tumor MR images particularly challenging. Methods To address these challenges, we propose a no-reference magnetic resonance curve estimation network named NR-MRC. First, a magnetic resonance curve estimation module uses nonlinear curve mapping to estimate spatially adjusted intensity and detail features without requiring reference tumor MR images. Second, a multi-scale feature estimation module extracts contextual features at different scales and fuses them with the initial estimates to generate enhanced MR images. Finally, a magnetic resonance scene statistics blind quality model evaluates feature consistency between the original images and their enhanced counterparts. Results Experiments on publicly available brain tumor and bladder cancer datasets demonstrate that NR-MRC outperforms the compared IQA and image enhancement methods. In the tested U-Net and DeepLab v3 settings, training with images selected by high NR-MRC scores or enhanced by NR-MRC increased segmentation metrics by approximately 20%. These task-specific gains do not by themselves establish improved clinical diagnostic image quality. Conclusion NR-MRC provides no-reference quality assessment and enhancement for tumor MR images and shows potential utility in the evaluated downstream segmentation tasks.

title: Weakly Convex Ridge Regularization for 3D Non-Cartesian MRI Reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose While highly accelerated non-Cartesian acquisition protocols significantly reduce scan time, they often entail long reconstruction delays for 3D data. Deep learning-based reconstruction methods can alleviate this, but typically rely on complex, highly parametrized architectures. Methods As an alternative, we introduce a rotation-invariant weakly convex ridge regularizer (WCRR). The resulting variational reconstruction approach is benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods on retrospectively simulated data and out-of-distribution prospective GoLF-SPARKLING and CAIPIRINHA acquisitions. Results Our approach achieves competitive reconstruction quality while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters and retaining the interpretability of a sparsity-promoting variational prior. Conclusion In summary, WCRR provides a compact and interpretable learned variational prior for 3D non-Cartesian MRI reconstruction.

originalAbstract:
Purpose

While highly accelerated non-Cartesian acquisition protocols significantly reduce scan time, they often entail long reconstruction delays for 3D data. Deep learning-based reconstruction methods can alleviate this, but typically rely on complex, highly parametrized architectures.

Methods

As an alternative, we introduce a rotation-invariant weakly convex ridge regularizer (WCRR). The resulting variational reconstruction approach is benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods on retrospectively simulated data and out-of-distribution prospective GoLF-SPARKLING and CAIPIRINHA acquisitions.

Results

Our approach achieves competitive reconstruction quality while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters and retaining the interpretability of a sparsity-promoting variational prior.

Conclusion

In summary, WCRR provides a compact and interpretable learned variational prior for 3D non-Cartesian MRI reconstruction.

title: Improved Upper-Airway Collapse Imaging in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Using Self-Supervised Spiral Variational Manifold Learning.
abstract: Purpose To propose a self-supervised variational manifold learning framework for dynamic upper-airway MRI reconstruction in obstructive sleep apnea from prospectively under-sampled spiral data during natural sleep, without requiring fully sampled training data. Methods A CNN generator and low-dimensional latent vectors were jointly optimized directly from prospectively under-sampled spiral k-space measurements, learning a subject-specific temporal manifold without an explicit motion model. A validation loss guided adaptive learning rate provided principled early stopping without ground truth. Eleven concurrent axial slices from velo-pharynx to hypo-pharynx were reconstructed at 183 ms temporal resolution and 11× acceleration across 8 OSA patients during natural sleep and 4 healthy volunteers performing the Müller maneuver. Reconstruction quality was compared against parallel imaging, compressed sensing, view sharing, and analysis-manifold reconstruction. Three expert raters independently assessed image quality using a four-point ordinal rubric. Results The proposed method resolved multi-site airway collapse across 11 contiguous slices, including simultaneous visualization of complete concentric retro-palatal collapse, lateral collapse at the velo-pharyngeal to oro-pharyngeal transition, and partial tongue-base and oropharyngeal narrowing. Expert scores were superior across aliasing, spatial blurring, and temporal blurring categories ( p<0.001 , pairwise Mann-Whitney U tests). Reconstructed airway dynamics were corroborated by concurrent respiratory effort and SpO 2 signals, with up to 13 obstructive events identified within a single imaging run. Reconstruction artifacts occurred in 8 of 132 slices (6%) and did not compromise airway visualization. Conclusion Self-supervised variational manifold learning demonstrates the feasibility of robust dynamic upper-airway MRI during natural sleep, with potential to inform future OSA phenotyping and surgical-planning studies.

title: Clinical Correlations Between Diagnostic Assessment Methods and Functional Outcomes in Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders are major contributors to pain, disability, reduced participation, and health-care utilisation. Structural and digital diagnostic tools can characterise pathology, but their ability to explain functional limitations and rehabilitation prognosis is often incomplete. This narrative review aimed to synthesise representative evidence on the relationship between diagnostic and screening methods and functional outcomes in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, with emphasis on clinical interpretation and practical use in care pathways. Methods Peer-reviewed literature, supplemented by manual screening of relevant reference lists, was reviewed to identify publications available through March 2026. The synthesis prioritised studies linking diagnostic findings to patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), performance-based tests, or real-world activity metrics. Results Conventional imaging, including ultrasound, computed tomography, and MRI, may identify clinically relevant pathology but often shows only modest concordance with pain, disability, and performance-based function. PROMs and brief performance tests provide the most direct functional anchors, whereas interpretation using the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) or responder thresholds is needed to distinguish statistically detectable associations from clinically meaningful change. Biomarkers and AI-supported analytics remain promising but insufficiently validated for independent functional prognostication. Wearable sensors appear most clinically useful for longitudinal monitoring of real-world activity, and brief psychosocial screening helps explain the discordance between structural findings and perceived disability. Conclusion Functional prognosis in musculoskeletal rehabilitation should not rely on diagnostic findings alone. A multidimensional, function-centred first-visit bundle combining focused examination, one region-specific PROM, one brief performance test, and brief psychosocial risk screening may improve triage, patient communication, rehabilitation planning, and follow-up. Diagnostic escalation should be selective and reserved for red flags, management-changing pathology, or failure to improve on repeated standardised functional reassessment.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Treatment of Peripheral Entrapment Mononeuropathies.
abstract: High-resolution neuromuscular ultrasound (US) is a valuable tool for the localization, diagnosis, and provision of conservative treatment to peripheral entrapment mononeuropathies. US-guided interventions require careful coordination of transducer and needle movement along with a detailed understanding of sonoanatomy. Preprocedural planning and positioning are instrumental in performing these interventions and should not be overlooked. Minimally invasive procedures, such as corticosteroid injections, aspiration of ganglia, orthobiologics, and hydrodissection, are useful options for the nonsurgical treatment of mononeuropathies refractory to conservative care. US is effective in determining atypical anatomy such as a bifid median nerve for improved accuracy and safety during injections, and precision based techniques such as hydrodissection may aid in physically separating the nerve from scar tissue and adhesions. The most well researched US guided treatment of entrapment neuropathy is carpal tunnel syndrome which demonstrates promising results from platelet-rich plasma, prolotherapy, hydrodissection, and percutaneous needle release. However, there is significant heterogeneity in procedure technique, injectate composition, injectate volume, and periprocedural conservative care that limits interpretation of the results and warrants continued head-to-head comparisons for research. This review highlights procedural details and outcomes for US-guided interventions of the most well-studied peripheral entrapment neuropathies. Despite many promising findings for these techniques, long-term outcomes and severe nerve compression may still benefit most from surgical decompression.

title: MRI-Derived Muscle Fat Fraction Reflects Disease Severity and Functional Impairment in Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease Type 1A.
abstract: Introduction/aims Progressive intramuscular fat infiltration is a hallmark of neuromuscular degeneration in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A). Quantitative assessment of muscle fat fraction (FF) by Dixon magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an objective biomarker of disease severity, but manual segmentation is laborious and variable. This study explored whether automated MRI-based FF quantification reflects disease severity and functional decline in CMT1A. Methods Sixty-nine genetically confirmed patients with CMT1A who underwent 3D multi-echo Dixon lower-leg MRI were retrospectively analyzed. A deep learning-based segmentation model delineated four muscle compartments (anterior, lateral, deep posterior, superficial posterior) and mean FFs were computed volumetrically. Correlations were tested between MRI-derived FFs and clinical outcomes, including the Charcot-Marie-Tooth Neuropathy Score (CMTNSv2), Functional Disability Scale (FDS), and time-, strength-, distance-, and repetition-based performance. Partial correlations were adjusted for age and body mass index. Results All compartmental and total FFs correlated positively with CMTNSv2 and FDS (r = 0.39-0.49, p < 0.05). FFs were positively associated with time-based and negatively with strength-, distance-, and repetition-based measures. FF Anterior showed moderate correlations with stair climb time (r = 0.68, p < 0.001) and 6-min walk distance (r = -0.66, p < 0.001), with similar magnitudes across compartments. Most associations remained significant after adjustment. The lateral compartment showed the highest FF (median 33.2%), consistent with the peroneal pattern of CMT1A. Discussion Automated MRI-based FF quantification provides a reproducible biomarker of disease burden in CMT1A, reflecting clinical severity and functional decline, and may serve as an imaging outcome measure in future studies.

title: Feasibility of Spin- and Gradient-Echo Dynamic Susceptibility Contrast MRI for Microvascular Characterization at 7 Tesla.
abstract: Perfusion MRI, especially dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC), is vital for glioma diagnosis and monitoring. While gradient-echo DSC is the current recommended implementation, combined spin- and gradient-echo (SAGE) DSC additionally allows for vessel size imaging (VSI) and has shown feasibility for microvascular characterization at 3 T. Higher field strength MRI offers increased contrast, resolution and signal-to-noise ratio, providing potential to improve microvascular characterization. This feasibility study aimed to implement a protocol for SAGE-DSC at 7 T and study its potential for microvascular characterization. SAGE-DSC was acquired in eight patients undergoing treatment for glioma (four females, median age 57 years) at 3 and 7 T. Data were analyzed using the temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and by comparing perfusion maps, VSI and vascular architectural imaging (VAI). Simulations were performed to study the relationship between vessel size and ∆R2* for SAGE-DSC at 3 and 7 T. Contrast agent dosage could be reduced while maintaining higher CNR at 7 T (but lower tSNR). Assessment by an experienced neuroradiologist showed similar rCBV map quality at 3 and 7 T. VSI maps showed the same normal-appearing gray-to-white matter ratios while in-plane resolution improved at least 52% at 7 T. VAI hysteresis loops at both field strengths traversed the same counter-clockwise direction, with increased loop areas reflecting increased susceptibility effects at 7 T. Simulations confirmed the higher sensitivity of gradient-echo and the higher specificity of spin-echo to the microvasculature, with peak spin-echo specificity moving from 3 μm at 3 T towards 1.5 μm at 7 T. This study confirmed the feasibility of using SAGE-DSC at 7 T for microvascular characterization. rCBV and VSI maps show similar behavior while allowing for reduced contrast agent dosage and improved resolution. The spin-echo specificity shifted towards smaller vessel radii for increasing field strengths. These findings form the basis for exploration and validation in larger patient populations.

title: Machine Learning-Based Development of Gadolinium Binding Peptides.
abstract: Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are indispensable tools in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), yet their clinical use is limited by non-specific tissue accumulation, low molecular specificity, and safety concerns. Protein and peptide scaffolds provide a promising alternative because they can bind metal ions with high selectivity and enable precise molecular targeting. However, identifying short peptide motifs with optimal gadolinium (Gd 3+ ) coordination and high relaxivity remains a major challenge. Here, we used a machine-learning-driven peptide evolution platform, the Protein Optimization Engineering Tool (POET), to design and optimize short Gd-binding motifs that enhance longitudinal relaxivity (r 1 ). Two algorithmic strategies were tested: motif-based and regular-expression-based representations. Both algorithms were trained on an initial set of 74 twelve-amino-acid peptides derived from natural EF-hand scaffolds. Through two rounds of directed evolution and experimental screening, POET predicted peptides with up to a 24% increase in r 1 ratio compared with the best natural EF-hand. Further analysis revealed that peptides exhibiting higher relaxivity generally possessed a more negative net charge and lower isoelectric point than the buffer pH, indicating stronger electrostatic stabilization of Gd 3+ . Sequence enrichment analysis showed that acidic and small polar residues, particularly aspartic acid, glycine, and threonine, were selectively favored during evolution, while bulky hydrophobic and basic residues were depleted. These compositional trends align with improved solubility and enhanced metal coordination. Together, these results demonstrate a generalizable framework that integrates computational evolution with biophysical screening to discover new biologically derived Gd-binding motifs. This approach provides a scalable route to engineer responsive, tunable, and biocompatible MRI contrast tags for precision imaging and molecular diagnostics.

title: Technical Feasibility of IVIM for Prostate Cancer Imaging Using High-Amplitude Whole-Body Gradient System With Spiral Readout and Velocity-Compensated Diffusion Encoding.
abstract: Intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) is sensitive to tissue diffusion and perfusion and has spurred great interest in various pathologies such as prostate cancer. However, poor repeatability and reproducibility of IVIM parameters hamper its wide-scale adoption in the clinics. To address this, improvements to the IVIM data acquisition and analysis are necessary. The purpose of this study was to develop a framework for high-quality IVIM imaging of the prostate. To boost signal precision and quality of IVIM parameter maps, we used a custom pulse sequence to combine velocity-compensated diffusion encoding with spiral readout at a high-performance 3 T MRI system with 300 mT/m gradients. IVIM parameters were evaluated in a cohort of five men with and without prostate cancer. Technical performance was assessed in terms of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), visual quality of IVIM parameter maps and parameter repeatability. High in-plane resolution images of the prostate were obtained with SNR > 3 (i.e., noise floor level) in 91% of voxels at the highest b-value of 500 s/mm 2 . The parameter maps exhibited high quality with fine features recovered in tissue diffusivity and perfusion fraction maps. Voxel-wise and ROI-based analysis revealed high repeatability of the parameters at single subject and group level across main prostatic tissue classes (peripheral and transitional zones) and prostate cancer. A combination of velocity-compensated diffusion encoding, spiral readout and strong gradients enables high-quality IVIM imaging in the prostate. Our framework may advance IVIM as a reliable imaging biomarker in prostate.
